# I N T R O D U C T I O N <note>original: "Prooemium"</note>

The Philosopher <note>This title refers to Aristotle, who was considered the ultimate authority on logic and science in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, the prince of philosophers, writes: "Man is the best of those things which are in the world." And "world" is taken here to mean all things contained within the sphere of actives and passives <note>In Aristotelian physics, this refers to the sublunary world where the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) interact and change.</note>, namely for the elements and the <term>elementated</term> <note>Things composed of the four elements.</note>. This having been presupposed, the proposition is proven. That thing is the best whose causes of generation are the most noble; but such is the case for man; therefore, etc. The major premise is clear, because an effect derives its nobility from its causes. The minor premise is proven regarding the matter of man.

Hence the matter of man, according to physicians, is posited to be the woman's menstrual flow together with the man's sperm, because both of these enter into the composition of man, just as milk is curdled <note>original: "coagulatur"</note> into the matter of cheese <note>The "rennet and milk" analogy was a standard way to explain how life was thought to form in the womb: the male seed acted as the "rennet" that gave form to the female "milk" or blood.</note>.

But natural philosophers posit that the woman's menstrual flow is the matter, and the man's seed is the efficient cause <note>original: "effectus", here used in the sense of the agency that produces the effect</note>, so that the man's seed stands in relation to the woman's menstrual flow as the craftsman to the craft-work, as Averroes <note>A famous 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> attests in the 7th book of the *Metaphysics*, in his "Digressions on Ideas." Likewise, in the *Physics* and the 5th book of the *Metaphysics*, chapter 10, he says that the man's sperm is reduced to the efficient cause; and in whatever way it is said, it is always clear that the matter of man is excellen... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely continuing as "excellent" on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page begins the treatise by citing Aristotle and Averroes to argue that human beings are the highest form of earthly life due to the nobility of their biological "causes." It explains the early scientific view of human conception through the analogy of milk curdling into cheese.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Averroes, biology, conception, Aristotelian physics, human nobility, efficient cause, medieval medicine</keywords>

# INTRODUCTION <note>original: "Prooemium"</note>

...most pure <note>original: "purissima", completing the word from the previous page</note> and the most noble among all seeds. Second, it is proven: that thing is best which, in its various parts, is made similar to the most noble body. But man is of this kind; therefore, etc. The major premise is clear, because this similarity follows the nature of the thing. The minor premise is proven because man is made like the heavens, in terms of the twelve signs of the zodiac. Three of these are "virtually" hot <note>In medieval science, "virtually" means possessing the power or quality of heat, even if not physically burning.</note>, namely Aries, Gemini, and Leo; to these correspond three members in man, namely the heart, the liver, and the testicles. Likewise, three are cold, namely Cancer, Taurus, and Virgo; and to these correspond the intestines, the bladder, and the diaphragm. Likewise, three are moist, namely Scorpio, Aquarius, and Pisces; to which correspond the brain, the stomach, and the lung. Likewise, three are dry, namely Capricorn, Sagittarius, and Libra; to which correspond the spleen, the gallbladder, and the kidneys. 

Hence he says in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics* <note>referring to Aristotle's work on the nature of reality</note> that the whole heaven is like a single contiguous composite. Therefore, we ought to be inclined toward the knowledge of this present book, which treats of human generation. Its <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The person who authored or produced the work.</note> is said to have been Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and one of the most influential medieval scientists and philosophers.</note>, who was sufficiently practiced <note>original: "tritus"</note> or rather, well-read in experiments <note>original: "experimentis"; here meaning observations or practical knowledge.</note>, and informed by women <note>Medieval medical texts often cited the practical knowledge of midwives and women as a source for understanding childbirth and generation.</note>. This is seen especially in the book *On Animals*, which he composed after he traveled the whole world with Alexander <note>Medieval legends often falsely claimed that Albertus Magnus traveled with Alexander the Great to observe the world's nature.</note>. And it is supposed
->that<- <note>original: "tur", the end of the word "supponitur" (it is supposed), serving as a catchword for the next page</note>

<summary>This page explains the "microcosm" theory, arguing that the human body is the most noble creation because its organs correspond directly to the twelve signs of the zodiac. It attributes the authorship of the text to Albertus Magnus, highlighting his reliance on both philosophical study and practical "experiments" or observations from women.</summary>

<keywords>zodiac, astrology, human anatomy, Albertus Magnus, Aristotle, Metaphysics, generation, elements, microcosm</keywords>

# INTRODUCTION <note>original: "Prooemium"</note>

->A 3<-

**T**o his beloved companion and friend in Christ, N. <note>a placeholder for a name, similar to "John Doe"</note>, a cleric of such-and-such a place: wishing him true wisdom and a continual increase of the present life.

*The subject of this book is "mobile being" <note>a standard Aristotelian term for physical things that change or move</note>, specifically focused on the nature of the secrets of women, so that when they are sick, we may be able to provide remedies; and when they are confessing, we may know how to assign the penances owed for their sins. It is divided first into two parts, namely the introductory and the main body <note>original: "executiuam," the section that carries out the actual instruction</note>. The main body begins at the point: "As it is written," etc. First, the author greets the person to whom he writes, saying, "I, Albert, residing in Paris, to his beloved companion and friend in Christ." Here the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>the agent or person who brings the work into being</note> is touched upon—both the one moving the work forward and the one being moved to act. The "moving" cause was a certain priest, who requested Lord Albert to write a book for him about the secrets of women. And this was because women are poisonous at the time of their menses, so much so that they poison animals with their gaze, infect children in their cradles, and stain mir[rors]* <note>The text ends mid-word: "specula" (mirrors). This refers to the medieval belief that a menstruating woman's gaze could dull a polished surface or harm living things.</note>

Albertus Magnus, On the Secrets of Women, Small Works of Nature, Introduction, menses, wisdom

<summary>This page introduces the text as a manual for a cleric, combining natural philosophy with practical medicine and pastoral care. It begins to explain the medieval theory that women become "poisonous" during menstruation, necessitating this specialized knowledge for priests.</summary>
<keywords>Albertus Magnus, secrets of women, menstruation, pastoral care, Paris, natural philosophy, efficient cause, medical remedies</keywords>

# INTRODUCTION

<meta>catchword: your</meta>

*...[they stain] a mirror that is well polished; and sometimes they cause the one who has intercourse with them to become leprous, and sometimes cancerous. And because evil is not avoided unless it is known, it is therefore necessary for those wishing to abstain from it to know the uncleanness of intercourse and many other things which are taught in this book. And so Albert, seeing that he <note>the priest mentioned on the previous page</note> asked justly, consented to him; and thus the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>the person responsible for making the book happen</note> is touched upon, being moved to act when it is said, "I write," etc. Wisdom is the knowledge of God and of eternal effects. And therefore the Philosopher <note>a common medieval nickname for Aristotle</note> says in the introduction to the Metaphysics: "Strictly speaking, there is no science of God" <note>original: "De Deo proprie non est scientia"; meaning God transcends human empirical study</note>. Likewise, nothing is better in this life, because through this wisdom we are made happy, as witnessed by Averroes <note>the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> in the prologue to the fourth book of the Physics. Therefore, the author writes for the increase of the present life; and he writes these things well for him, because through wisdom, a man is rendered praiseworthy to God and to men.*

When your favorable and gracious company asked me that I might more clearly reveal certain things which are hidden and secret regarding the nature and condition of women, having seen your petition, no laziness held me back from the compilation of this brief and concise little treatise, once the material was obtained. But although I have a small and youthful mind, which is drawn to other matters according to its capacity and the opportunity of the time, I am nevertheless desiring to satisfy your appe- <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "appetitui," meaning "desire" or "request"</note>

<summary>This page explains the moral and medical necessity of studying the 'secrets' of women—namely to avoid disease—and begins the formal authorial dedication citing Aristotle and Averroes.</summary>
<keywords>leprosy, menses, Albertus Magnus, Aristotle, Averroes, Metaphysics, wisdom, medical ethics, medieval science</keywords>

# PREFACE

->A 4<-

...to whom I write this present letter, in which you will find many things concerning the requests [made], partly in a **philosophical style**, and partly in a **medical style**, as seems appropriate to the subject matter. <note>The author distinguishes between "philosophical" (theoretical causes of nature) and "medical" (practical application for health) approaches.</note> For I have written this, asking for your steadfastness, so that you might be resolute and secretive regarding this work and business, lest you permit any boy—whether in age or in character—to come into its presence. <note>A common warning in medieval "books of secrets," suggesting that the content is too mature or dangerous for the "youthful" or morally undisciplined.</note> And if you do this, I promise to reveal more to you about these and other things, and to transmit [knowledge] with the present work and art for a medical purpose, which I shall provide at greater length, God willing.

*Here he shows the cause which might excuse him from the labor of this task, and the meaning is clear from the text. Note that the author says a **youthful and small mind** <note>original: "mens iuvenilis & pusilla"</note> held him back; here he avoids arrogance, because a mind is called "small" when it is imbued with small conditions of knowledge. # ON THE GENERATION
## OF THE EMBRYO.
### CHAPTER I.

**A**fter our preceding discourse has directed the listener’s attention toward the subject matter of this work, it is now timely to descend into the substance of the work itself, and first to examine the generation <term>original: "generatio"; the process of coming into being or being born</term> of the embryo. Regarding this, it must be carefully noted and committed to memory that every human who is naturally generated is produced from the father’s seed and the mother’s menstrual matter, according to the consensus of all philosophers and physicians. I specifically mention "physicians" because **Aristotle** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose biological theories were central to medieval science</note> did not believe that the father’s seed actually became part of the physical substance of the fetus; instead, he claimed that the fetus arises solely from the menstrual matter, and he posits that the seed afterward evaporates away like a vapor <note>Aristotle's "hylomorphic" view: the male provides the form/soul like a carpenter, while the female provides the wood/matter</note>. The physicians, however, state that the entire seed—both that from the father (which is called sperm) and that from the mother (which is called the menstrual matter)—enters into and becomes the physical substance of the fetus.

*The first chapter of the operative part, in which he intends to approach the subject matter, namely to demonstrate the generation of the embryo or fetus. It is not* <margin>This marginal note serves as a summary, indicating that the text has moved from the introduction to the "executive" or practical part of the book.</margin>

<summary>This page introduces the biological process of human generation, highlighting a major scientific debate between Aristotle's theory—that the male seed only provides a "spark" and then vanishes—and the medical view that both parents contribute physical substance to the fetus.</summary>

<header>On the Secrets of Women</header>

...the controversy between **Physicians** and **Philosophers**.

For the **philosophers** <note>Specifically followers of Aristotle, who believed the male provides the "blueprint" but not the physical building blocks</note> say that the seed of the man, when joined with the menstrual matter of the woman, relates to that menstrual matter just as a **craftsman** <term>original: "artifex"; an artist or skilled worker</term> relates to his **work**. Hence, just as a **carpenter** is only the **efficient cause** <term>original: "efficiens"; the agent or force that brings something about</term> and the house is the **effect**—such that he alters and arranges the material of the house—so too the man's sperm alters the woman's menstrual matter into the form of a human. 

They posit this because they observe that after the father’s "corruption" <note>original: "corrupto"; in medieval physics, this refers to the end of one state of being to begin another; here, it means the father's active role has concluded</note>, the generation of the human and the transformation of the woman’s seed takes place; therefore, one must posit an efficient cause so that, even after the father’s part is done, the woman's menstrual matter may be transformed. And because the "end" and the "effect" do not coincide <note>meaning the tool or the builder does not physically stay inside the finished product</note>, the man's sperm does not enter into the physical matter.

But the **physicians** <note>Referring to the medical tradition of Galen, which held that both parents contribute physical substance</note> say the opposite: namely, that a human is created from the most noble matter. Therefore, for the seed to enter the matter of the woman's fetus—as it is a surplus of the **second digestion** <term>original: "secundæ digestionis"; a stage in the medieval metabolic process where food-turned-blood is further refined into nutrients or reproductive fluids</term>—the man's sperm is better "cooked" <note>Refined by the body's natural heat</note> and digested; thus, it must enter into the matter and substance of the fetus. This is evidenced by the fact that the fetus sometimes **resembles the father** in the genitals and in many other traits; this would not be possible unless his sperm entered the actual substance of the fetus.

Likewise, the physicians say that in the man's seed there exists a certain **begetting spirit** <term>original: "spiritus gignens"; a vital, breath-like force or "pneuma" believed to carry the power of life</term> which penetrates the entire matter of the joined seeds, and that spirit is the shaper of all the limbs...

## ALBERT THE GREAT’S BOOK

*Just as a **blacksmith** <note>original: "faber"; a craftsman who works with fire and metal</note> shapes iron with a hammer, so that **vital spirit** <term>original: "spiritus"; in medieval medicine, a subtle gas or "breath" that moves through the body to perform biological functions</term> arranges and softens all the limbs, and through that spirit the **efficient principle** <note>The active force or "worker" that creates the child</note> is preserved. But the **Philosophers** <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> posit that the man's seed evaporates like vapor, because the **womb** <term>original: "matrix"; the uterus</term> is a very porous organ; thus, after the formation of the fetus, the heat of the sun <note>Medieval biology often linked the "heat" of the body to the heat of the sun/stars</note> causes the man's seed to evaporate and recede from the womb through the pores. That the womb is porous is evident, because the child receives nourishment through these pores. It is also evident because the womb is a skin, and every skin in an animal is porous, for otherwise sweat could not exit without pain—which is false, since in heat the pores are opened, and then sweat exits, and then hairs also grow out through the pores. Note, the **embryo** is a certain **fleshy mass** <term>original: "massa carnea"</term> gathered from these seeds, and that fleshy mass is transformed into the formation of the fetus.*

Having seen these things and accepted one part of the opinion of **Aristotle** or the **physicians**, we must see by what method and how those seeds are received in the woman. To this it must be said that when a woman conceives, the menses are retained for this final cause <term>final cause: in Aristotelian philosophy, the "causa finalis" is the purpose or goal for which a thing exists—in this case, the nourishment of the child</term>: so that the fetus existing in the woman's womb can be nourished from the retained menses. 

However, when a woman engages in intercourse with a man, she experiences great pleasure because the nerves and veins within the vulva <note>In medieval anatomy, "vulva" often referred to the entire internal and external female reproductive tract</note> are rubbed and moved by the male member <note>original: "virgam virilem"</note> present there. Thus, the vulva dilates and emits fluid. This is natural in the context of intercourse, as that act is itself natural. It is, however, something of a "forced" <note>original: "violentus"; in a philosophical sense, this means a movement caused by an external force or stimulus rather than the body's internal timing</note> action compared to the regular natural flow of the menses. 

Furthermore, from the nourishment taken every day, a substance is created that is naturally suited to be expelled during intercourse. And this resolves the doubt as to why pregnant women so greatly desire intercourse: the desire for intercourse arises from the abundance of this superfluous matter <note>Medieval medicine taught that "superfluous" or leftover nutrients from digestion were transformed into reproductive fluids</note> derived from food. Therefore, because the menses are retained and new matter is generated every day, the woman desires intercourse intensely, for the woman's vulva grows warm from the abundance of that matter, and thus she craves the act.

...it must be discussed from which parts of the body <term>members: "membra" in medieval anatomy refers to organs or limbs</term> sperm is separated in men, and similarly the "menses" in women—taking "menses" here to mean the seed that is emitted during intercourse <note>original: "coitu"; medieval science often believed women produced a "seed" during climax that contributed to generation</note>. 

And it seems that it comes from every part of the body, because the fetus resembles the parents in all its parts. 

But on the contrary, if this were so, it would follow that a person with imperfect parts would produce a child with imperfect parts, which is false. The falsehood is clear through experience: if a father were blind, lame, or mutilated in a finger, he would not always produce a child like himself. The logic of this is self-evident.

It must be said that in intercourse, those seeds are separated from four principal parts <term>principal members: in the Aristotelian and Galenic tradition, these are the "noble" organs—the brain, heart, liver, and the reproductive organs—which govern all bodily functions</term> namely from the brain, the heart, the liver, and the womb in women, and from the testicles in men. 

Consequently, they come from other parts as well, but not from those other parts of the body primarily. And by this, it is said in response to the objection <note>the objection mentioned above regarding why children look like their parents</note> that the fetus resembles the parents. I say it is sufficient that the seed comes from the principal organs, insofar as those organs influence the other parts of the body; and the seeds are especially separated and distinguished from the brain. 

Hence we see that those who engage in intercourse frequently suffer from headaches, and their limbs especially become dried out, and their vision is greatly weakened <note>Medieval medicine taught that because sperm was "separated" from the brain and vital organs, excessive sexual activity would drain the body of its vital moisture and heat, particularly affecting the eyes and head</note>.

# ON THE FORMATION OF THE FETUS.

## CHAPTER II.

**H**aving seen these things, we must return to the formation of the fetus in the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note>. The first matter received in the womb has the nature of milk for the first six days. The natural heat released in the man’s sperm, as well as the heat of the womb, acts upon this "milk," so that the matter becomes white like milk. Then, that matter is transformed into the nature or color of thick and somewhat well-cooked blood, and this lasts for nine days; after that time, the consolidation of the fetus's members <term>members: "membra," referring here to the distinct limbs and organs</term> occurs over the next twelve days.

*This is the second chapter of the active part of the book, in which the author returns to the topic of how a fetus is formed. A doubt arises as to whether the heat of the seed <note>original: "spermatis"</note> is elemental fire, or if it is celestial heat, and similarly regarding the heat of the womb, etc. There are various opinions on this. But according to Aristotle in the second book of "On Animals," it must be said that this heat is animal, or celestial <note>In medieval science, "elemental heat" (like a candle flame) was thought to destroy or consume, while "celestial heat" (like the sun) was a life-giving force</note>. The reason is that elemental heat is destructive, but celestial heat is the preserver of animals according to Averroes <note>Averroes was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to medieval university learning</note> in the 12th book of the "Metaphysics," commentary 12.*

<summary>This page outlines the early stages of embryonic development, describing a timeline where the "seed" transforms from a milky substance to thick blood before the limbs begin to take shape. It also includes a philosophical debate on whether the heat required for this process is biological (celestial) or physical (elemental) in nature.</summary>

### 34. THE BOOK OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS

...from matter and form, the **accidents** <term>accidents: in medieval philosophy, these are non-essential qualities of a thing—like its color, size, or ability to move—that don't change what the thing fundamentally is</term> within it will be named in a threefold way. And first he prefaces certain things, then secondly he pursues his intention there. For from the last **Note**, that conclusion is formed from the text: The fetus is formed successively by the planets. The same is proved thus outside the text: A fetus is formed according to that which influences the being and living of the fetus in different ways; but the planets are of this kind, therefore, etc. The minor premise is evident, because to one fetus it influences living for a long time, and to another for a short time, as is clear through **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose works were the foundation of medieval science</note> in his **Centiloquium** <note>original: "Centiloquio" — a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>, and through his commentator **Haly** <note>likely Haly Abenragel or Haly ibn Ridwan, famous Arabic astrologers whose commentaries were essential to Latin scholars</note>.*

Note, the soul moves the body; through this movement the soul is first moved by something else, namely by that which is **desirable**, and thus it moves...*

->C 2<-

...stirs the **spirits** <term>spirits: in medieval physiology, these were subtle, invisible vapors that carried out the commands of the soul through the body</term>, which once moved, they themselves move the **muscles**, which when moved, move the **limbs** <note>original: "membra"</note>. And so it is clear that the **appetible** <note>original: "appetibile" — the object of desire or the goal the soul seeks to reach</note> is the primary mover.

But a doubt arises: whether any **accident** <note>a non-essential quality, like color or heat, as opposed to the "substance" or essence of a thing</note> can be the primary source of any **substance**. **Walter Burley** <note>original: "Galterus Burbalii," a famous 14th-century English philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> responds in his commentary on the *Fourth Book of Sentences* that it can be so; and we prove it thus: an "agent" is that which destroys one thing and creates another. Such is the **imbalance of humors** <note>original: "humoris indispositio"</note>, or the disproportion of the elements, which destroys the **form of a man** and creates the **form of a corpse**, which is a substance; therefore, etc. 

The response given is that this "notifying humor" is actually a kind of substance. For "humor" here is not used to mean an accident, but is taken to mean **offending humid matter** <note>original: "materia humida peccante" — a medical term for bodily fluids that have become diseased or unbalanced</note>; thus, an accident does not destroy a man except by the power of the underlying matter. But when it is said, "Nothing is contrary to substance," the answer is that this is true regarding **perfect contrariety** <note>the idea that a substance, like "water," has no direct opposite in the way "hot" is the opposite of "cold"</note>; however, it is certainly true for **diminished contrariety**, which is sufficient for the destruction of one thing and the creation of another.

*Also, the text says that an **accident** <term>accident: in medieval philosophy, a property or quality that is not essential to the nature of a thing (like being tall or tan), as opposed to its "essence" (like being human)</term> is not sustained in a **simple essence** <term>simple essence: a substance that is not made of physical parts, such as a soul or a spiritual being</term>. The reason is because an accident arises from the nature of the subject, involving not only the scale of the subject (or its material cause) but also the scale of the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the agent or force that brings something into being</term>. Therefore, the **composite** <term>composite: a being made of multiple parts, specifically the human union of body and soul</term> is a material cause according to one part, and an effective cause according to another part. And because one cannot lay these out within a simple essence, a simple essence is not a subject for accidents—especially real accidents—even though a simple essence could be the subject of its own "modes of being," just as **prime matter** <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless substance that has the potential to become any physical thing</term> is the subject of its own potential, which is its own proper and formal mode of being. From this it is clear that the potential for accidents does not belong to the soul alone, but is an accident of the whole composite person. However, they are said to belong to the soul because they are present in the body principally by means of the soul.*

<header>OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS</header>

...and light, but both motion and light produce heat; therefore, etc. I respond that every planet exerts an influence of heat, but one more, another less. Thus Saturn and the Moon exert the least heat compared to the other planets.

But from this a doubt immediately arises, because someone might doubt whether Saturn rules in the conception of every embryo. And if not, then what has been said is surprising.

*Here he raises a doubt: if what was said were true, it would follow that Saturn always rules, and this would be surprising. The logical consequence is not proven in the text itself, but is self-evident, because the conception of children occurs every day.* <note>The commentator is pointing out a potential logical flaw: if Saturn is required for the first month of every pregnancy, but pregnancies begin every day, it might seem as though Saturn must always be the dominant astrological ruler, which contradicts the system of rotating planetary hours.</note>

Regarding this, it must be noted that **prime matter** <term>prime matter: in medieval science, based on Aristotle, this is the fundamental "stuff" of the universe that has no form of its own but can become anything when acted upon by celestial forces</term> is subject to the celestial bodies and their motions. And this is what the **Philosopher** <note>original: "Phil.", referring to Aristotle, who was so central to medieval thought he was often called simply "The Philosopher"</note> says in the first book of **Meteorology** <note>Aristotle's *Meteorologica*, a treatise on natural phenomena</note>: that all lower things are caused by higher things and are governed by their motions. And therefore it is necessary that these lower things be regarded both particularly and universally by the higher ones, understanding this as the power of the entire celestial body. For universally these lower things are regarded by the higher ones because nothing is made of elementary matter except by the power of the celestial bodies. Therefore the **Commentator** <note>original: "Commentator", referring to Averroes (Ibn Rushd), the 12th-century scholar whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to medieval university education</note> says in the second book of **Metaphysics** <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysica*</note> that nature does not act except [under their] gover- <note>The text cuts off here due to the page break; the full word is likely "governance."</note>

# THE BOOK OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS

Note, the text speaks of **bodies with uniform parts** <note>original: "corpora similium partium." In medieval science, these are "homeomerous" substances, like water or gold, where every small piece is identical in nature to the whole, unlike complex organs like a heart or hand.</note>. These are called "uniform" because any part of them can be described by the name of the whole. This is understood in terms of physical quantity: for example, any part of a fire is still called "fire." However, fire also possesses parts of different natures, namely the **matter** of the fire and its **form** <note>Aristotelian "hylomorphism" suggests everything is a combination of matter (the "stuff") and form (the organizing principle or essence).</note>. Now, the generation of these uniform parts—found both in the **elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> and in things composed of elements—is governed and determined by the movement of the celestial bodies.

The same must be said regarding the planets and individual living beings. For this reason, it happens that people might die in one part of the earth, but if they were in another part, their lives could be sustained or "revived." For if a **mixed body** <term>mixed body: any physical substance, such as a human body, composed of a mixture of the four elements</term> becomes excessively hot while in an already hot region, it ought to be moved to a cold region so that its heat may be balanced or "tempered"; then, it would be restored to health.

Therefore, since matter is primarily subject to the "super-celestial" bodies, it is necessary that it receives the form of a specific species as determined by a specific part of the heavens. It cannot receive this form from the celestial body in a general or "common" way. This is because such a general influence would regard all matter and all forms indifferently; if the heavens gave one form for a general reason, they would give all other forms for that same reason. This is because all forms which exist as **potential** <note>The capacity to become something.</note> in **prime matter** <term>prime matter: the fundamental, formless substance that has the potential to become any physical thing</term> and in the **First Mover** <term>First Mover: the ultimate cause of all motion in the universe, providing the initial "push" for everything else</term> are already **actualized** <note>The state of being "real" or "complete."</note>, as he says...

*Here the author proceeds regarding the other planets in relation to the formation of the fetus. It seems that the planets do not form the matter of the fetus in this way, because there is said to be a proportion* <term>proportio<gloss>a correspondence or direct relationship</gloss></term> *between cause and effect; and if this were so, it would follow that the generated embryo would be eternal, since the planets themselves are eternal. In the third month Mars arrives, who with his heat and dryness forms the matter, separating the arms from the sides, and separating the neck from the arms, and forms the head; and the third month is attributed to this operation.

*Note: Mars is hot and dry, and therefore he has the role of forming the legs and arms, which are dry. For it is necessary that sufficient heat gathers the dry earthy parts if legs and arms are to be made. Note that from the text we have it that the head is formed earlier by Mars than the heart is by the Sun. The cause of this, according to physicians, is because all the principles of life are in the head, therefore it is formed first. But Aristotle posits that the heart is formed first, because the heart flows* <note>original: "fluit." ...because Aries itself is the beginning of vital operation, so too is the head, in which all the powers of the soul flourish. Therefore, physicians say that the <term>vegetative power<gloss>original: virtus vegetativa</gloss></term> <note>In medieval philosophy, the vegetative power is the aspect of the soul responsible for basic biological functions like growth, nutrition, and reproduction.</note> of the body is located principally and determinately in the head, but originally in the heart. 

But there is a doubt: does life consist more in the heart than in the head? It would seem to be in the head, as is evident through the writings of **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in medieval Europe.</note>, who says he saw a ram walking even after its heart had been removed. This could not happen unless life had its beginning in the head. 

But against this is **Averroes** <note>An influential Andalusian philosopher (1126–1198) known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the sixth book of the *Physics*, who mocks him, saying that he himself saw a ram running here and there after its head had been cut off. Therefore, Averroes maintains that life is principally and originally in the heart, but consequently in the head. 

Physicians, however, are very much guided by the senses; this is because they see that the senses of the powers are located in the head. For this reason, they say life consists principally in the head, but it is not so; rather, it is in the heart. 

But what shall we say to the author of the text, who says that the head is the more noble part of the body? It must be said that this is true according to appearance and the greater activity of the <term>vital spirits<gloss>original: spirituum vitalium</gloss></term>, because the operations of life appear more in the head than in the heart. Hence, there is no doubt that nature placed the more noble and better part of the body in the middle of the body; for the heart is the first thing living and the <insert>last</insert>... <note>original: "ultimum" (from catchword). This refers to the common medieval adage that the heart is "primum vivens et ultimum moriens"—the first to live and the last to die.</note>

Here the author pursues his intention. <note>This refers to the author continuing his systematic explanation of the celestial bodies and their natures.</note> And it is divided into seven parts, following the fact that there are seven planets. <note>In the medieval geocentric model, there were seven "wandering stars": the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> Note that **Saturn** is the highest planet, and it completes its course in 30 years; thus it returns to the same point of the **Zodiac** from which it began. And according to Ptolemy and Master <term>Rabbi Moses<gloss>original: "Rabi moysen," referring to Maimonides, the influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and astronomer</gloss></term>, Saturn is the highest planet and is the most distant from the earth. So great is this distance that to reach the part where it touches the <term>sphere of Jupiter<gloss>In medieval cosmology, planets were believed to be embedded in nested, transparent spheres</gloss></term>, a man would have to travel from the earth for five thousand, seven hundred and thirty-four years, seventy-seven weeks, and three days—assuming that a man’s <term>day’s journey<gloss>original: "dieta"</gloss></term> was ten miles.

And according to the astronomers, Saturn is of such great magnitude because it is ninety times larger than the whole earth. Likewise, it is stated in the text that Saturn is very slow in its motion; this should be understood to mean that it completes its course in a longer period of time. Hence, Saturn is easily thirty times larger than the Sun in terms of its **orb** <note>In this context, "orb" refers to the circumference of the planet's circular path or sphere, rather than the physical body of the planet.</note>. Just as the Sun traverses its own orb by its own motion through the signs of the Zodiac in one year, so Saturn does in 30 years; and thus it actually moves as quickly as the Sun. For example: if two men were walking, and over thirty days one walked thirty miles while the other walked only one mile, then the one who walks one mile... <note>The text ends mid-analogy; the author is explaining that Saturn's "slowness" is an illusion caused by the massive scale of its orbit compared to the Sun's.</note>

Likewise, one born under **Mars** is of a reddish color with a certain darkness, because the color red is caused when heat acts upon moisture; by consuming the moisture, it leaves behind what is dry. We see this when bricks are to be fired: before they are burned they are not red, but afterward, once the moisture is consumed, they are made red. Such people have small eyes, because the eye is an organ in which moisture flourishes; the eye is of a watery nature on the outside, as is clear from the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima". This refers to Aristotle’s influential work on biology and psychology, where he discusses the composition of the sense organs.</note>—which is evident if the eye is injured, for water flows out. Because **Mars** is hot and dry, he cannot form large and beautiful eyes. 

Likewise, **Mars** induces wars because he dries out the brain and sets the heart on fire, and thus anger is generated around the heart. Hence, anger is the kindling of the blood around the heart, and for this reason **Mars** was called the **God of War** according to the ancients. He is also deceitful. The reason is that because he is dry and hot, he is always irascible and thinks of evil, so that he may deceive and betray men. Likewise, he greatly desires sexual intercourse because he is hot, but he is capable of little because he lacks the necessary moisture.

The **Sun**, indeed, being a regal star, the light of the world and called the "eye of the world," makes one born under him fleshy, with a beautiful face and large eyes, and a white complexion with a certain redness.

# ON THE GENERATION
## OF IMPERFECT
### ANIMALS.

### CHAPTER IV.

**I**n order that those things which have been said may be understood in a clearer light, and how sometimes many fetuses are formed in the womb and many children are born, such as twins, it is appropriate to digress a little from the generation of man, and we must look at the generation of imperfect animals, which are not generated from seed, but from <term>putrefaction|The medieval theory of "spontaneous generation," which suggested that "lower" life forms like insects or maggots could arise directly from decaying organic matter without parents.</term>. Accordingly, it should be noted that imperfect animals, such as flies and the like, are not always generated in the same way as perfect animals, because they are not generated through the <term>separation of seed|The process by which the "matter" of a child was thought to be shed or separated from the parent's body during conception.</term>, but from putrefied matter, as is clear in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Metaphysi." A reference to Aristotle's work. While the *Metaphysics* deals with the nature of existence, the author is likely drawing on the Aristotelian idea that nature does nothing in vain.</note>.

*Chapter four, in which the author treats the formation of the fetus in the womb, and first makes a digression from his purpose. Secondly, he returns to the purpose, where we respond that flies and spiders are imperfect animals; they do not belong to the perfection of the universe, yet they are not altogether in vain, because nature herself has ordained that they absorb bad <term>humors|The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that medieval science believed determined a person's health and personality.</term>, so that humans might be better preserved from bad humors.*

<page-num>77</page-num>

<header>ON THE SECRETS OF WOMEN</header>

Whether the same animals are generated from seed or without seed is a matter of doubt among many. For the opinion of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were standard texts in medieval European universities.</note> in his book *On Floods* <note>original: "lib. de diluuiis"</note> is that the same animals can be generated both from seed and without seed. He explains this by stating that a universal flood could still occur, and in such a flood all living beings would be destroyed. Once all living beings were destroyed, celestial influences <note>The medieval belief that the stars and planets influenced the physical transformation of matter on Earth.</note> would act upon the corpses of the dead that have putrefied, and then, by the power of heaven, the same types of creatures that existed before would be generated again. Thus, one individual would be generated from putrefied matter, and another would later be generated as its likeness in species through the <term>separation of seed|The emission of reproductive material during copulation, which was thought to "separate" from the parent's body.</term>. Therefore, the same species can be generated from seed and without seed.

He demonstrates the possibility of this through the senses <note>meaning through physical observation or experiment</note>, saying: if the hairs of a menstruating woman are taken and placed under rich earth where manure has lain during the winter, then in the spring or summer, when they grow warm from the heat of the Sun, a long and strong serpent will be generated. That serpent will then further generate its own kind in species through the separation of seed. The same thing is shown in the case of the mouse; for at one time, a certain mouse was created from putrefaction, and it subsequently generated its own likeness in species from seed. Many more reasons could be brought forward, but the aforementioned examples suffice, as it would be tedious to relate all the occurrences pertaining to that matter.

In winter, manure is sufficiently moist and warm from within because the surrounding cold does not allow the innate heat to evaporate or escape.*

...they do this by saying: Everything that is generated **univocally** <term>univocally|generation where the offspring is the same species as the parent, such as a human begetting a human</term> is generated from something like itself in species. This is true either **formally** or **virtually**, as has already been said <note>original: "formaliter aut virtualiter." In medieval science, "formal" means the offspring looks like the parent; "virtual" means the parent or cause contains the power to create the offspring even if they don't look alike.</note>. *Here he solves the doubt and responds according to his own intention. Note that according to Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the famous scholar and theologian to whom this text is attributed.</note>, this is the manner of the generation of animals from **rot** <term>putredo|The process of decay or decomposition</term>: because when the heat of the Sun is extended down to the rotting matter, it then extracts a subtle moisture from that matter, and certain small skins are generated so that the interior heat is not allowed to escape.*

*And then, by the power of the Sun, that heat which is in the rotting matter seeks an exit and is blocked; and from such a movement upward and downward, a certain **pulsating spirit** is generated: by means of which spirit, life is produced in such matter. And if it is asked whether that pulsating spirit is a **substance** or an **accident** <note>In the philosophy of the time, a "substance" is a thing that exists by itself (like a rock), while an "accident" is a property that needs a substance to exist (like the color of the rock). To call the spirit a substance means it has its own physical/spiritual reality.</note>, it must be said that it is a substance. For that spirit acts by means of a **formative power**; and because a cause only produces a substance by means of a spirit, it is therefore necessary for that spirit to be a substance. And that spirit is a subtle body, generated from the finer part of the matter by means of rot.*

I prove this through experience: I take a **rotting mouse** and place it in a location where the solar rays are at their full strength; I find that the heat of the sun causes the entire substance of the mouse to evaporate, so that nothing remains there except the skin. 

Note that in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, **generation** is divided into two types: some is **univocal**, and some is **equivocal**. **Equivocal** generation occurs when the generator and the offspring differ in species, such as if a mouse is generated from the earth <note>original: "si generatur mus de terra." And from this, the saying of **The Philosopher** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), who was simply called "The Philosopher" by medieval scholars.</note> in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* is explained, where he says: *Everything that is made, is made from its like in species.* This is true regarding univocal generation, but not equivocal. ## CHAPTER VI.

**J**ust as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>A Greek philosopher whose works on biology and physics were the standard textbooks for medieval scholars.</note> says in the second book of the *Physics*, just as there is <term>error</term> <note>original: "peccatum"; while this often means "sin," in a biological context it refers to nature "missing the mark" or a "failure" to reach the ideal form.</note> in nature, so there is also in art. The explanation of this principle is very useful for our present business and for making our intentions clear, as far as is now necessary. This can be seen in humans who have only one foot, or only one hand, and so on regarding others...

...in others. It must be noted, however, that this marvel, which <term>Philosophers</term> <note>Scholastic scholars who studied Aristotle's works on nature and physics.</note> call a **monster of nature**, happens in many ways: for it occurs either from a **deficiency of matter**, or from an **excess**. 

Regarding deficiency, it happens in several ways. In the first way, the deficiency is attributed to the <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia"; in medieval science, this refers to the physical substance—often thought to be menstrual blood—that provides the "building blocks" for the fetus.</note> itself. In this case, since the principal members <note>The "principal members" are the vital organs like the heart, liver, and brain, which were believed to form first.</note> must be formed and organized first in the child, **wise and ingenious nature** <note>original: "natura sagax & ingeniosa"; medieval thinkers often personified Nature as a clever craftsman doing her best with the materials available.</note> acts as completely as she can. She forms those parts which are principal, and once these are formed and arranged, she applies herself to the formation of the other members. There, using the matter she has, she does what she can; she forms a diminished part when there is a deficiency in the matter, and thus an **error** <note>original: "error"; a biological failure to achieve the perfect human form.</note> occurs. 

Because of this, it sometimes happens that the **head** is larger or smaller than the nature of that particular individual being generated requires. For if the deficiency in the matter had not hindered the part preceding the formation, the head thus formed under that deficiency of matter would have been proportional to the individual nature in itself and in all other members. This same conclusion can be drawn regarding the other principal organs, since a specific order is owed to these principal parts, as the <term>natural philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophi naturales"; those who studied the physical world and biology.</note> and **physicians** <note>original: "medici"; medical practitioners whose theories were based on the balance of bodily fluids.</note> testify. In another way, indeed, the deficiency of matter is attributed specifically to some particular part that is to be generated.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the causes of biological anomalies. The previous page established that "monsters" arise from either a deficiency or an excess of reproductive "matter." This page provides a specific analogy for how Nature prioritizes vital organs when resources are scarce.</meta>

<page-num>103</page-num>
->## ON THE SECRETS OF WOMEN ##<-
->G 4<-

Here the author pursues his intention regarding the method of generating <term>monsters</term> <note>original: "monstra"; in medieval science, this term referred to any birth that deviated from the "perfect" human form, without the modern negative connotation of a "creature."</note> in nature and introduces a simile. He argues that nature is likened to art, because just as a craftsman first forms and builds a good foundation, and afterwards strives to build upon that foundation, so similarly nature first forms the **principal members** <note>The vital organs believed to be the seat of life and heat.</note> and those most necessary: namely the **heart**, **liver**, **brain**, and **testicles**; <note>In medieval anatomy, "testicles" often referred to both male and female gonads (ovaries), as they were seen as analogous organs.</note> and afterwards the less principal ones, namely the **hands**, **feet**, and **arms**. Thus, if there is a deficiency in the matter, it is better for the principal parts to be formed than the less principal ones. 

Note that nature is twofold: one is **intending**, the other **producing**. Now, intending nature <note>The "ideal" plan or blueprint of nature which always seeks perfection.</note> does not err, because she always intends what is best. But producing nature <note>The actual physical process of growth which must work with imperfect material.</note> sometimes errs, but this is on the part of the matter being either abundant or deficient, such that monsters are created according to a **deficiency of matter**. 

This happens in two ways: either according to <term>discrete quantity</term>, <note>original: "quantitatem discretam"; a mathematical category referring to things that can be counted individually.</note> as when someone is sometimes born with only one foot, or with four fingers on one hand; or according to <term>continuous quantity</term>, <note>original: "quantitatem continuam"; referring to things that are measured in size or volume rather than counted.</note> and thus someone is born with an excessively large head, or with an excessively large hand. If, however, this occurs through **abundance** <note>An excess of reproductive "matter" or "blood."</note> of matter, it is also in two ways: either according to discrete quantity, thus sometimes there is generated...

<summary>This page explains that Nature acts like a craftsman, prioritizing the formation of vital organs (heart, brain, etc.) over limbs when biological material is scarce. It also introduces the Scholastic distinction between the "ideal plan" of Nature and its actual physical execution.</summary>

*Here the author presents an objection or an instance, and solves it in the text. For which, note that a force regularly intending to produce something can be hindered by **particular nature** <note>original: "naturam particularem"; the specific physical conditions of an individual's body or womb, as opposed to the general laws of the universe.</note>, and therefore it is clear that **monsters** <note>original: "monstra"; in medieval medicine, this referred to any birth that deviated from the natural norm, such as twins or physical deformities.</note> are not intended by nature, except perhaps by accident. Also note, particular nature does not intend the ends of **privations** <note>original: "privationum"; the state of lacking a natural quality or "failing" to reach a complete form.</note>, because it sees that it is better to be than not to be. But God and the celestial nature know how to arrange all things best, and this is called the **unerring intelligence** <note>original: "intelligentia non errans"; the belief that the movements of the stars and the divine mind are perfect and never make mistakes, even if earthly matter fails.</note>. Whence from the first book of **On the Heavens** <note>Aristotle’s "De Caelo," a standard text on the nature of the universe.</note>, all death, corruption, sickness, and infirmity are contrary to nature.*

**If a woman emits little or no seed, it is a sign that she has conceived.**

Here the author explains the signs of conception. The reasoning for the first sign is that when a woman conceives, her **natural heat** <note>original: "calor naturalis"; a vital energy in medieval medicine believed to power digestion, growth, and reproduction.</note> rushes inward from the rest of her body to help form the fetus; because of this, coldness is left behind in the limbs. We see a similar thing happen when a person eats: after eating, they feel cold because the natural heat moves to the stomach to digest the food. For this reason, one should not study immediately after a meal, but should first do a little work to warm up, and then study once the digestion is strengthened. This is because at the time of study, the **vital spirits** <note>original: "spiritus vitales"; subtle substances thought to circulate through the body to carry out life functions.</note> rush to the brain to assist it. 

This is also evident in those suffering from fevers, who have thick **humors** <note>original: "humores"; the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that medieval doctors believed governed health.</note> in the stomach which the natural heat intends to digest. The heat goes to the stomach, and so those with fever feel cold externally; but then as the heat recedes back from the stomach, they suffer from great heat. 

The author assigns a reason for this second sign: because the **womb** <note>original: "matrix"; the standard Latin term for the uterus.</note> closes up and does not allow the **seed** <note>original: "semen"; medieval medical theory often held that women, like men, produced a "seed" or generative fluid during intercourse.</note> to pass through or escape. Note that young women, who take the greatest pleasure in the act of **intercourse** <note>original: "coitu"</note>, are able to emit seed and conceive, but this is not the case for older women. Likewise, at the time of intercourse during conception, nature retains the seed internally so that it does not exit, and this is for the sake of the fetus.

# ON THE SIGNS OF CHASTITY.
## CHAPTER X.

**T**he signs of chastity are these: shame, modesty <term>verecundia: a sense of bashfulness or moral reserve</term>, and fear, along with a chaste gait and speech, and a disdainful manner when dealing with men and the affections of men. However, some women are found to be so clever <note>original: "astutæ"; this reflects a common medieval trope regarding women’s ability to deceive men about their sexual history.</note> that they know how to fake all these signs. In such a case, a person should turn instead to the urine, because the urine of virgins is clear and bright—sometimes white, and sometimes glaucous <term>glaucous: a pale, shimmering grey-green or blue-grey color</term>. If, however, the urine is golden in color, clear, and heavy, it contains a sign of a joyful spirit—that is, of sexual desire <note>original: "appetitum"; referring to a natural inclination toward intimacy.</note>—and this is true even in those who have not been corrupted.

For corrupted women <note>original: "corruptę"; women who have experienced sexual intercourse.</note> have turbid <note>original: "turbidam"; cloudy or stirred up.</note> urine, caused by the previous breaking of the thin skin <note>original: "pelliculæ"; the hymen, as discussed on the previous page.</note>, and a man's seed appears at the bottom of such a woman's urine. But in menstruating women, the urine is blood-colored, and during the month when she suffers this flow, she has watery eyes, a different color in her face, and feels a loathing for food. And therefore, let every man beware that he does not have intercourse with them at that time, because it is harmful <note>Medieval medicine held that conception during menstruation could lead to diseased offspring or harm the male partner.</note>. Wherefore prudent women know how to guard themselves then, and they remain separate from men during the time of the menstrual flow.

# ON THE IMPEDIMENTS TO CONCEPTION.
## CHAPTER XII.

**N**ow let us touch upon some things regarding the impediments to conception, which are many. An impediment sometimes occurs from too much humidity <note>In medieval medicine, "humidity" or moisture was one of the four qualities that needed to be balanced for health. An "overly moist" womb was thought to be too slippery to hold the seed.</note> of the womb, sometimes from too much coldness, sometimes from dryness, and sometimes on account of too much fatness of the body. This is because the fatness wrapped around the <term>opening of the womb</term> <note>original: "orificio matricis." Historically, this refers to the cervix or the entrance to the uterus.</note> constricts it and does not permit the man’s seed to enter.

The recognition of this condition is found in a woman whose <term>kidneys</term> <note>original: "renes." This often refers generally to the loins or the lower back area where fat deposits were observed.</note> are buried and hidden in fat on every side. For if those women receive seed during <term>intercourse</term> <note>original: "coitu"</note>, it cannot enter the womb, and thus they eject it along with the discharge of urine.

And therefore, briefly, if such a woman's urine is inspected after intercourse, it will be manifest whether the man’s seed has been collected in her womb or not. If it has not entered <note>literally "if so" (si sic), referring back to the seed being ejected</note>, then her urine is impure because of the mixture from the man. 

But if it appears again—and sometimes it will appear that the urine did not totally eject that seed because the women are warm—then they exhale <note>The text suggests that excess bodily "heat" could cause the reproductive fluid to evaporate or dissipate like a vapor.</note> it by their own heat. There are also certain women who have such tender and <term>slippery</term> <note>original: "lubricas." Suggesting a womb that is too smooth or overly lubricated to allow for the "grip" necessary for conception.</note> wombs that se- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "semen" (seed).</note>

*Here the author sets down the second instruction. And note that when a woman has conceived, she is then weakened* <note>The text ends here mid-sentence; the catchword "litatur" at the bottom of the original page indicates the next page begins with the completion of the word "debilitatur" (is weakened).</note>

# BOOK OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS #

Having spoken somewhat of the **menses** <term>menstruum</term> <note>referring to menstrual blood, discussed on the previous page</note>, we must now transition to the matter of **sperm** <term>sperma</term> in the male. **Sperm**, indeed, as was stated above, is nothing other than the surplus of nourishment that does not turn into the substance of the thing being nourished. Regarding this, it should be noted that physicians posit four **digestions** <term>digestiones</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" refers to any process of cooking, refining, or transforming a substance within the body.</note> in a human being. They say that the method of nutrition is such that, first, food chewed in the mouth is directed from the mouth to the stomach itself. There, the first digestion occurs, and the pure "earthy" part is separated from the impure "earthy" part; that impure part is directed to the bowels and is later emitted through **excrement** <term>secessum</term>.

But this pure part is further directed to the **liver** <term>hepar</term>, and there the second digestion occurs. And then, once again, the pure "watery" part is separated from the impure "watery" part. The impure watery part is directed to the bladder and is later emitted through **urination** <term>mictura</term>, but the pure part is directed to the heart, where the third digestion occurs, and the pure is separated from the impure. This impure part is directed to the seminal vessels, and from that, **sperm** is made in the male, and in the female, the **menses**; but the pure part is **blood** <term>sanguis</term>. This blood is directed from the heart through the large veins, which are called **capillaries** <term>capillares</term> <note>While we think of capillaries as tiny vessels, medieval writers often used this term to describe the fine, hair-like branchings of the major veins that reach the limbs.</note>, through which the blood is directed to individual members <note>meaning the limbs and organs</note>. In those members, the final digestion occurs, and again the pure is separated from the impure; the impure is emitted through sweat, through the nails, and similar things. This pure part, however, remains...

<summary>This page explains the medieval physiological theory that sperm and menstrual blood are the "impure" surplus of the third stage of digestion, occurring in the heart, while the body's members perform a fourth digestion for growth.</summary>

...is turned and congealed into the substance of nourishment, so that those pores which were emptied by **natural heat** <term>calor naturalis</term> are, conversely, refilled there. 1.  **Sufficient matter**, which is bread and the like.
2.  **Drink**, which receives that **fourth digestion** <term>quarta digestio</term> <note>In this system, the fourth digestion is the final process where blood is transformed into the actual tissues of the body.</note>.
3.  **Distributing nature**, which moves the nutrients.
4.  **Natural heat**, which converts the nourishment into the nourished body.

*Here the author proceeds to the final objective of the book and demonstrates the method of the **generation of sperm** <term>generatio spermatis</term>.*

*Note that the human being is of the best and most subtle digestion because he possesses great heat; and because of many labors, he digests and consumes moisture, for heat acts upon moisture as its subject. Heat causes the **radical moisture** <term>humidum radicale</term> <note>Radical moisture was thought to be the "lamp oil" of life—an innate fluid present from birth that sustains the body's heat. When it runs out, the person dies.</note> to evaporate. Therefore, there must be a restoration of heat <note>original: "restauramentum caloris", likely meaning restoration of the fuel for heat</note> lest it consume the radical moisture, for then death would follow. Once the radical moisture in which life consists is consumed, no medicines are of any use.*

*However, it should be noted that a specific individual can, through some medicine, live for a year or more without nourishment, as has been experienced; but this cannot happen through the common course of nature. Note that **mastication** <term>masticatio</term> is a certain crushing of food performed by the teeth. Thus, nature ordained sharp teeth in the front part so that they might easily divide the food, but in the back, she ordained wide teeth for the sake of chewing.*

*There are thirty-two eating teeth of a man.* <note>This Latin verse is likely a mnemonic device used by students to remember basic human anatomy while studying the larger philosophical text.</note>

But from these things which have been said, a certain doubt arises: whether heat acts upon moisture by consuming it, just as the operation of heat acts in that which is called **natural heat** <term>calor naturalis</term>. Regarding this, it should be known that according to **Aristotle** <term>Aristoteles</term> in the fourth book of his *Meteorology* <term>Meteorologica</term> <note>Aristotle’s "Meteorologica" was a standard university text that covered not just weather, but the chemical-like interactions of the four elements and qualities.</note>, in the chapter on operation, there is a threefold operation of heat considered in the section on the operation of active qualities.

The first operation of heat, insofar as it is heat, is to dissolve, evaporate, and gather together **like substances** <term>homogenea</term>, and to scatter **unlike substances** <term>heterogenea</term>. The second [operation] is evident, because if a mass of gold and silver is taken and placed in fire, the heat causes the gold to flow away from the silver and vice versa. 

And thus the **Philosopher** <note>In the Middle Ages, "The Philosopher" almost exclusively referred to Aristotle.</note> spoke in the second book of *On Generation* <term>De Generatione</term>, where he says that a specific heat acts like a tool—namely, like an axe or a double-edged hatchet—which always dissolves things that are joined. 

But heat, insofar as it is **natural heat**, possesses within itself the **formative power** <term>virtus formativa</term> <note>This was the biological force believed to be responsible for shaping an embryo or a plant according to its species.</note> of each thing or nature of which the heat is said to be natural; and thus within it is the power of the heavens, or the power of the **celestial movers** <note>The "movers" were the spiritual or cosmic intelligences believed to guide the rotation of the planets and influence life on Earth.</note>, and the force of the seed, the **complexion** <term>complexio</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determines a person’s health and personality.</note>, or the form of that nature which it shapes. Just as it happens to be seen in the heat within the seed of a plant or animal, where there is a force called the "form of the plant." And he adds that because of these **passions** <note>In this context, "passions" refers to physical urges or the tax that sexual activity takes on the body's systems.</note>, males are shorter-lived than females. For it is generally true that males are longer-lived than females, provided they have not been sexually active.

Thus, from the philosopher's intent, it is clear that human life consists fundamentally in **heat and moisture** <term>calido & humido</term>, although it involves other things instrumentally and ministerially <note>This means that while organs (instruments) and biological processes (ministers) perform the work of living, the essential "fuel" of life is the balance of heat and moisture.</note>; and so it is clear that intercourse dries the body. It is also clear that when the cause preserving an effect is present, the effect itself remains. If, however, the cause were destroyed, the effect would also be destroyed. Therefore, from first to last, intercourse which occurs in excess is the cause of a short life, etc.

The twelfth herb is called **Colorio** or **Coloricon** by the Chaldeans, **Clamor** by the Greeks, and is commonly named **Sage** <note>original: "Salvia"; *Salvia officinalis*</note> by the Latins. If this herb is allowed to rot beneath dung inside a glass vessel, it procreates a certain worm or a bird having a tail like that of a blackbird. If anyone is touched upon the chest with the blood of this creature, they will lose their senses for fifteen days or more. And if the aforementioned serpent <note>Although previously called a worm or bird, the text now uses the term "serpent," common in medieval alchemy to describe transformed biological matter</note> is burned and its ash is placed in a fire, there will immediately be a terrifying flash of thunder. Furthermore, if the aforementioned powder is placed in a lamp and lit, it will appear as though the entire house is filled with serpents. This has been tested by modern practitioners.

The thirteenth herb is called **Olphanas** by the Chaldeans, **Hiliorion** by the Greeks, and **Vervain** <note>original: "Verbena"; *Verbena officinalis*</note> by the Latins. As the **Magi** <term>ancient priest-astrologers whose names were often invoked to lend authority to magical texts</term> report, if this herb is collected while the sun is in the sign of **Aries** <note>The Ram; the first sign of the zodiac, associated with the beginning of spring</note> and combined with a grain of one-year-old **Peony**, it cures those who suffer from the "falling sickness" <note>original: "caducos à malo morbo"; a historical term for epilepsy</note>. If it is placed in rich soil, after eight weeks worms will be generated; if these worms touch anyone, that person will die immediately. If the aforementioned herb is placed in a dovecote, all the doves will gather there. And if the powder of these worms is placed in the sunlight, it will appear as though the sun is a bruised, bluish-black color <note>original: "lividus"</note>. Moreover, if the powder is placed in a place where people live, or lies between two lovers, it immediately causes strife or malice between them.

**The fourteenth herb** is called **Celeyos** by the Chaldeans, **Casini** by the Greeks, and **Melisophilos** <term>literally 'Bee-lover'; identified as Lemon Balm (*Melissa officinalis*), so named because bees are attracted to its scent</term> by the Latins, of which **Macer** <note>original: "Macer"; referring to Macer Floridus, the pseudonym of a medieval author who wrote a popular verse herbal in the 11th century</note> makes mention. And if the aforementioned herb is tied around the neck of an ox, it will follow you wherever you go. **The fifteenth herb** is called **Eglerifa** by the Chaldeans, **Ysaphinus** by the Greeks, and **Rose** <note>original: "rosa"</note> by the Latins, and it is a plant whose flower is very well known. And if the aforementioned items are placed near a net, fish will gather there. Moreover, if a **magaris** <term>likely referring to a specific type of lizard or a fish; medieval texts often used this term for creatures believed to have restorative powers</term> should be dead, and it is placed in the aforementioned mixture for half a day, although it is not truly restored <note>original: "licet tamen non acquiritur"; implying the effect may be a semblance or temporary</note>, it will recover life. And if the aforementioned powder is placed in a lamp and then lit, all people present will appear black in the manner of Satan <note>referring to a demonic or blackened appearance, a common "parlor trick" in medieval natural magic</note>. Furthermore, if the aforementioned powder is mixed with olive oil and with quick-sulfur <note>original: "sulphuræ vivo"; also known as virgin sulfur, which has not been processed by fire</note>, and a house is anointed with this while the sun is shining, the entire house will appear to be in flames.

Concerning this stone, it is written in the readings of the philosophers that when worn on the finger or the neck, it makes travelers safe and welcome to their hosts. It also induces sleep because of its cold nature, and the sapphire-like variety possesses this quality specifically.

The **Eagle** is a well-known bird; it is called "Gluttonous" <note>original: "Vorax"</note> by the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>an ancient people of Mesopotamia, frequently cited in medieval magic as masters of secret wisdom</note>, and *Rimbicus* by the Greeks. <term>Aaron and Evax</term> <note>traditional pseudo-authorities often cited in medieval lapidaries and bestiaries</note> report that it possesses a marvelous nature or power: if its brain is ground into powder and mixed with the juice of <term>hemlock</term> <note>a highly poisonous plant, *Conium maculatum*</note>, those who eat this will immediately seize themselves by their own hair and will not let go until they are carried away. The reason for this effect is that the brain is exceedingly "hot," so much so that it generates a **fantastic power** <note>original: "virtutem fantasticam"; in medieval science, this refers to the power of the *phantasia* or imagination to create images</note> by blocking the bodily passages with its vapors.

**Casso** <note>original: "Casso"; likely referring to the Beaver, usually called *Castor*</note> is a well-known animal; it is called *rapa* by the Chaldeans, but is called *Orgalo* by the Greeks. Regarding this animal, Aaron says that if its feet are carried by anyone, that person will never grow weary but will always desire to move forward. Likewise, whoever carries its feet shall always be victorious and shall be feared by his enemies. He also says that its right eye, wrapped in the skin of a wolf, renders a man pleasing, graceful, and kind. Furthermore, if a food or a powder is made from the aforementioned things and given to someone in their food, they will love the giver dearly. This last point has been proven in our own time. If the aforementioned mixture is placed in dung, venomous worms are produced; if anyone should eat these, they will immediately fall asleep.

The **Owl** <note>original: "Bubo"</note> is a well enough known bird; it is called *Magis* by the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>a term often used in these texts to denote ancient Babylonian or magical wisdom</note>, and it is called *Hissopus* by the Greeks. The powers of this bird are marvelous. For if its heart and its right foot are placed upon a person while they are sleeping, that person will immediately tell you whatever they have done, and whatever you ask of them; and this has been tested by our brothers <note>likely referring to the Dominican Order, to which the author Albertus Magnus belonged</note> in modern times. Furthermore, if someone places these same parts under their armpit, no dog will bark at them, but will instead fall silent. And if the combination of the aforementioned parts, along with its spirit <note>original: "anima"; likely a reference to a specific organ or a prepared extract of the bird's essence</note>, is hung from a tree, birds will flock together at that tree.

The **Goat** <note>original: "Hircus"</note> is a well-known beast; it is called *Erbichi* by the Chaldeans and *Masai* by the Greeks. If its blood is taken while warm and mixed with vinegar and the juice of <term>fennel</term> <note>original: "fœnationis"; probably a variant of *foeniculum*, fennel, though it could refer to hay-juice</note>, and is boiled together with glass, it renders the glass as soft as dough; it can then be thrown against a wall or stone partition and it will not break. 

And if the aforementioned mixture is placed in a vessel and used to anoint someone's face, marvelous and horrible things will appear to them, and it will seem to the person that they are about to die. Furthermore, if the mixture is placed in a fire, and someone suffering from the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "caducus"; an old term for epilepsy</note> is present along with an accompanying <term>magnet stone</term>, they will immediately fall to the earth as if dead; but if <term>eel water</term> <note>original: "aqua anguillarum"; water in which eels have been washed or boiled</note> is given to them to drink, they will be cured immediately.
