The **Camel** is a well-enough known animal; indeed, it is called *Cyboi* by the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>a term used in medieval texts to refer to ancient Babylonian or magical wisdom</note> and *Iphim* by the Greeks. If its blood is placed upon the head inside the skin of a <term>spotted lizard</term> <note>original: "stellio"; a gecko or lizard with star-like spots, often used in medieval magic</note> while the stars are shining, it will seem as if that person is a **Giant**, and that his head is in the heavens. This is stated in the book *Alcorath* <note>a magical text attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus</note> by Hermes. Similarly, if anyone should eat of this <note>the camel's blood</note>, they will immediately go out of their mind. Furthermore, if a lamp is greased with its blood and lit, it will seem as if all the people standing around have the heads of camels—provided that there is no other light coming from another candle.

The **Hare** is a well-enough known animal; it is called *Veterellum* by the Chaldeans, and truly called *Onolosam* by the Greeks. Its power is reported to be wonderful. <term>Evax</term> <note>a legendary King of Arabia and author of an influential book on the powers of stones</note> and **Aaron** <note>likely referring to a Jewish physician or alchemist cited in medieval scientific works</note> say that its feet, when joined with a stone—or in another version, with the head of a <term>blackbird</term> <note>original: "merula"</note>—move a person to audacity, so much so that they do not fear death. And if it is tied to the left arm, the person may go wherever they wish and return safe and sound without danger. Furthermore, if it is prepared for eating along with the heart of a **Weasel**, the person will not cry out from then on, even if they were being killed.

The **Squirrel** <note>original: "Experiolus"; likely a Latinization of the Old French 'escuriel'</note> is a well-enough known animal. If its claw is burned and <term>ground up</term> <note>original: "consolidetur"; literally 'made firm' or 'consolidated', implying a preparation of a solid mass or powder</note> and given in food to any horse, that horse will not eat for three days. And if the aforementioned <note>claw</note> is placed with a little bit of <term>turpentine</term> <note>original: "terebentiva"; a resin from trees used in medicine and chemistry</note>, it will be bright, and afterward it will become like a little <unclear>cloud</unclear>.

### THE BOOK OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS

...actions, until a great part of these marvelous works appeared sufficiently. At last, however, there occurred to us a matter of ultimate wonder and strangeness, which appears almost imperceptible to nearly all common and ordinary men: that is, the <term>binding; the magical practice of restraining or influencing others</term> of men and their powers through incantations, through <term>characters; magical signs, symbols, or sigils</term>, through sorceries <note>original: "veneficia"; while literally "poisonings," in this context it refers to harmful magic or potions</note>, and words, and many very useful things which do not seem at all possible, nor appear to have a sufficient cause. 

And when these things had long troubled the mind, we found a probable explanation in the natural philosophy of Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was an influential Persian polymath whose theories on how the soul could project power outside the body were used to explain magic naturally</note>. He suggests that within the souls of men there exists a certain power of changing things, and that other things are obedient to it when the soul is carried away by a great excess of love or hatred for something. 

Therefore, when the soul of someone is carried into a great excess of any passion, it is found by clear experience that the soul itself binds things and alters them toward the very thing it desires. For a long time, I did not believe this. But after I read books of <term>necromancy; the magical art of communicating with spirits or performing ritual magic</term>, and books of "images" <note>referring to the creation of astrological or magical talismans</note>, and magic, I found that the operation of the human soul is the greatest root of all these things. Because of a great emotion <note>original: "affectionem"</note>, the soul alters its own body and the other things it intends—whether because other lower things obey it due to its inherent dignity, or because a suitable hour <note>referring to the astrological "hours" discussed in previous chapters</note> coincides with such an intense emotion...

We know from this, therefore, that certain people cannot be bound, since they are more fervent <note>more intensely passionate or spiritually "heated"</note> themselves than those acting against them. Universally, he binds who burns with greed or intense desire, and he is dissolved who is more strongly seized by or directs himself toward that release. They perform this, therefore, with the things the soul dictates to itself, in that specific hour and toward those people. After it was confirmed by the Philosophers that all species <note>original: "species"; here meaning the essential types or categories of things</note> of things move and incline toward things like themselves, since there is in them an active rational virtue <term>virtus activa rationabilis; a purposeful power or inherent energy</term> by which they act and move both toward themselves and toward different things; fire moves toward fire, and water toward water. And now Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were foundational to medieval European science</note> says that while something stays in salt for a long time, it becomes salt; and if something stays in a foul place, it becomes foul; and if it stays with someone bold, it becomes bold; and if with someone timid, it becomes timid. And an animal that stays with humans becomes human-like and domestic; and generally it is verified from reason and experiment <term>experimento; knowledge gained through observation or trial</term> that every nature moves toward its own species. This specific nature becomes known in the primary qualities <note>the fundamental properties of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, and similarly in the secondary, and it was the same in the tertiary; in all dispositions, there is nothing that does not move toward its own kind according to its whole power. After this was implanted in the minds of the philosophers <term>philosophorum; here referring to natural scientists and thinkers of antiquity</term>, they themselves discovered the dispositions of natural beings <term>entium naturalium; the inherent qualities or "settings" of living things</term>. They certainly knew that in certain beings a great coldness is innate; in some, along with this, a great boldness <term>audacia</term>; in some, great anger <term>iracundia</term>; in some, great fear <term>timor</term>; in some, an innate sterility <term>sterilitias</term>; in some, an innate heat of love <term>ardor amoris</term>; and in others, some other innate power <note>original: "virtus"; in a medieval context, this refers to an inherent efficacy or medicinal/magical property</note>.

No one can deny that every single thing is full of wonder, though you may not know which thing possesses the greater marvel until it is carefully examined. However, most people tend to despise that which they know nothing about, and thus such things hold no value for them. For every thing possesses its own unique balance of heat and cold <note>In medieval science, "heat" and "cold" were two of the four primary qualities (along with moisture and dryness) that determined the nature of all physical matter.</note>, and the wonders of fire are no more remarkable than those of water; they are simply different and of another kind. Likewise, the wonders of pepper are no greater than those of henbane <note>original: "iusquiami"; Henbane (Hyoscyamus niger) is a toxic plant in the nightshade family, often used in medieval medicine and folklore for its narcotic properties.</note>, though their effects are distinct. 

Anyone who believes that the wonder of things arises from heat and cold cannot deny that a great wonder exists in every thing, since every thing possesses the particular heat and cold that is appropriate to its nature. And he who believes that the wonder of things resides in the stars and their "aspects" <note>The relative positions and angles between planets, believed to influence events and objects on Earth.</note>—from which objects draw their marvelous and hidden properties—can be certain that every thing has its own suitable celestial figure, from which its marvelous power of operation arises. For everything that begins under a specific ascendant <note>The sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment, such as a birth or the beginning of a process.</note> and celestial influence starts its existence by drawing into itself a unique efficacy for producing and performing wonderful things. Furthermore, those who believe that the wonders of things arise through "friendship" <note>In this context, "friendship" refers to "sympathy," the natural attraction or harmony between two different substances.</note> cannot likewise deny the existence of "enmity" <note>Or "antipathy," the natural repulsion between substances, such as the wolf and sheep mentioned previously.</note>. Universally, according to every school of philosophy, every single thing is full of wonders. And after...

A large portion of the Philosophers and physicians believed that the entire marvelous nature of experiments <note>In this context, "experiments" (experimentorum) refers to practical applications of knowledge, recipes, or observed phenomena.</note> and wonders emerged from natural things when they are brought into the light through **heat** and **cold**, **dryness** and **moisture**. They designated these <term>four qualities</term> <note>The primary properties of the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, Earth) which were thought to be the building blocks of all physical matter.</note> as the roots of all wonders, and held that their mixing is required for every marvelous thing. And yet, when they found many experiments of the Philosophers that they were not able to verify through heat and cold—indeed, the result was often the opposite—it happened that they wondered incessantly and grew saddened; and for the most part, they deny the phenomenon, even if they see it with their own eyes.

They have verified that the quality of wonder proceeds from things in very diverse ways. Often it is through heat and cold, and often through other virtues <note>In medieval science, a "virtue" (virtus) is an inherent power or property of an object, such as a magnet's "virtue" to attract iron.</note> innate to things alongside their **substantial forms** <note>The essential nature or "soul" of an object that makes it what it is, according to Aristotelian philosophy.</note>; and often through the relationship that things have to one another. For this reason, the wonders of things are rendered incomprehensible [to the unlearned], as the author says. Often by their own nature <note>original: "per se"</note> they produce one effect, while by accident <note>original: "per accidens"; referring to an indirect or unintended result that occurs because of a specific circumstance.</note> they produce the opposite—often directly, and often indirectly. Rightly, therefore, <term>Plato</term> said that he who is not highly skilled in <term>Dialectics</term> <note>The art of logical reasoning and debate used to uncover the truth.</note> and learned in the virtues of natural things—likewise in the signs of the stars and **necromantic virtues** <note>In this context, this refers to the "science of images" or the hidden powers within nature that can be manipulated, rather than modern "necromancy" involving the dead.</note>—will not see the underlying logic of wonders, nor will he himself know them, and he will not share in the **treasure of the philosophers** <note>original: "thesaurum philosophorum"; a common term for the secret, ultimate wisdom or the goal of the Great Work in alchemy.</note>.

I know, therefore, that every thing possesses qualities from heat and cold: this is the sign from which one thing makes another effective by accident, both directly and indirectly. And it possesses each virtue from the stars and the figure of its generation <note>The specific astrological alignment at the moment a thing was created or born.</note> which it exerts in mortality, construction, and its agreement with others; and yet, each thing has virtues related to itself, through which each thing is the source of a marvelous effect.

Since, therefore, every nature moves toward its like, one can imagine how wondrous effects might be applied to every operation. And in the *Book of Decoration* <note>original: "lib. decorationis," likely referring to a manual on cosmetics or female health.</note>, take the quantity of a bean of <term>alcibh</term> <note>A term of likely Arabic origin referring to a specific medicinal substance, possibly a plant or mineral used in alchemy.</note> and soak it in the urine of a mule and give it to the woman to drink, and she will not conceive.

And if someone anoints the vent of a rooster with oil, he does not mate with the hen, nor is he able to; and if someone wishes that the rooster should not crow, let him anoint its head and forehead with oil.

The Philosophers say that if anyone removes the heel-bone of a female **weasel** <note>original: "mustela"</note> while it is still alive, and it is hung upon a woman, she will not conceive as long as it remains upon her; but when it is removed, she may become pregnant.

And the Philosophers have found that if a certain woman is sterile, when they apply a thing that causes sterility <note>This refers to the principle of "similia similibus curentur" or like-cures-like; using a contraceptive substance to jump-start fertility in a sterile person</note>, the woman becomes fertile; and vice-versa.

If two testicles of a **weasel** are taken, bound, and tied to the leg of a woman, and she carries the bone <note>the heel-bone mentioned previously</note> with her, the woman will not conceive. And it is said that when a **sponge** is thrown into wine mixed with water, and then it is pulled out, squeezed, and pressed, the water comes out of it and the wine remains; but if the wine is not mixed, nothing comes out <note>This is a common medieval scientific "experiment" used to explain the separation of elements</note>.

**Tabariensis** <note>Referring to Al-Tabari, a 9th-century Persian physician and scholar</note> says that if a **sponge-stone** <note>original: "lapis spongiæ," likely a calcified growth found in sponges or a piece of pumice</note> is hung around the neck of a child who suffers from a violent cough, his cough is soothed. And when a **beetle** <note>original: "scarabeus"</note> is put into the head of a donkey, or its anus, the beetle **falls into a trance** <note>original: "fyncopizat," from the Greek for "syncope" or fainting; it describes a state of suspended animation</note>, and it does not recover until it is pulled out from there.

And if a person eats **lentils** and is then bitten <note>presumably by a venomous animal</note>, the bite is not healed. And when [something] is put into the anus of a tall **ram** or an **elk** <note>original: "arietis altis sive alcis"</note>, its wool falls out.

It is also said that if any stone is tied to the tail of a **donkey**, it will neither roar nor bray <note>original: "non rugit nec rudet"</note>.

And they said that when you wish that flies do not approach a house, then put <term>condisum</term> <note>original: "condisum," likely a corruption of *conyza* (fleabane), a plant known for repelling insects</note> and **opium** in whitewash <note>original: "albedine calcis," literally the whiteness of lime</note>, and then whitewash the house with it; then the flies will not enter at all.

And they say that the skin of a **donkey**, when it is hung over children, prevents them from being frightened.

And <term>Archytas</term> <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and scientist; here cited as an authority on natural magic</note> says that if the wax from the left ear of a **dog** is taken and hung over those suffering from periodic fevers, it helps greatly, especially with the **quartan fever** <note>original: "quartanæ," a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note>.

And the philosophers say that any species or individual that has never suffered a sickness helps against every sickness; and when a specific pain has never been present [in them], it aids and heals a person of that pain.

#### On Illusory Smoke

For all who are in the dwelling will appear to themselves as if they are great men in the forms of horses and elephants; it is truly a great marvel.

### A Lamp for Silencing Frogs
A lamp which, when it is lit in a place where frogs are found, causes none of them to make a sound: instead, they all remain silent as long as it is lit. Take the **fat of a crocodile** <note>original: *pinguedinem cocrodili*</note>, and prepare it with **wax** that has been whitened in the sun, and fashion a **wick** <term>wick: Latin *licinium*, the cord or material that draws fuel to the flame</term> from it. Light it in the place where the frogs are: and when they see this light, they will immediately fall silent.

### A Lamp for Visual Illusions
Another lamp which, when lit, makes those standing around appear to one another like statues or stones. Take **vitriol** <term>vitriol: Latin *zimat*, an alchemical term often derived from Arabic *zaj*, referring to metallic sulfates used as pigments or reagents</term> and grind it well. Then take a **funeral cloth** <note>original: *pannum funeris*</note> and moisten it with **fish fat** or with **pure sesame oil** <note>original: *oleo sisamino*</note>. Place this in a **green lamp**, and put a small amount of that ground medicinal powder upon it, and the effect is marvelous. 

### A Wick for Joyous Madness
A **wick** which, when lit, causes people to never stop dancing, rejoicing, and becoming frenzied with joy—and this is especially true of women. Take the **blood of a certain bird** called a **Solon** <term>Solon: likely a lapwing or a species of plover; medieval texts often associated bird blood with specific temperaments</term>, which resembles a turtle-dove, and mix it with an equal half-portion of blood from a **sea-turtle** <note>original: *turturis maris*; in this context, it may refer to a sea-bird or a specific marine creature</note>. Soak the wick in this mixture and light it in the middle of a house where there are singers and young women; this is marvelous and has been proven.

### How to carry fire in your hand without harm

If you wish to carry fire in your hand so that it does not hurt you: Take **lime** <term>lime: Latin *calcem*, specifically quicklime or calcium oxide</term> dissolved in warm **bean water**, and a little **magranculis** <note>This term is likely a corruption of *malicorium* (pomegranate peel) or *manganaria*, ingredients commonly found in medieval "fire-walking" recipes</note> and a little **marshmallow** <term>marshmallow: Latin *malvavisci*, the plant *Althaea officinalis*, known for its mucilaginous, soothing properties</term>. The philosophers say that such lime does not burn in fire, and **fish glue** <note>original: *glutem piscis*, often used as a binder</note> protects from fire, as do **Yemeni alum** <term>Yemeni alum: Latin *alumen jamenum*, a specific mineral salt used as a mordant and fire-retardant</term>, **salamander blood** <note>In medieval lore, the salamander was believed to be immune to fire and capable of extinguishing it</note>, and **soot** from a furnace or a kettle. Therefore, when a liniment is made from all or some of these things, fire does not cause injury. **Egg white** and marshmallow are also helpful in this regard.

### On the generation of dragons and fearful visions
Philosophers say that the **sinciput** <term>sinciput: the front or upper part of the skull</term> is the primary part of the head, and from a human sinciput, shortly after death, **worms** <note>original: *vermes*; likely referring to maggots appearing through spontaneous generation, a common medieval belief</note> are generated. When seven days have passed, those worms become **flies**, and after fourteen days, they become **great dragons**. If one of these bites a person, they will die immediately. 

However, if you take matter from this <note>original: *ex ea*; referring to the dragon or the decomposing material</note> and cook it with **oil**, and make from it a candle for a **bronze lamp** using a **wick** made from a **funeral cloth**, you will see through its light a great wonder and forms that cannot be described, accompanied by an intense fear.

### A wondrous experiment for handling fire
A **wondrous experiment** <note>original: *experimentum mirabile*; a standard term in medieval science for a practical test or recipe</note> that allows men to walk into fire without injury, or to carry fire or **glowing iron** in their hand without harm:

Take the juice of **marshmallow** <note>original: *bismalua*; Althaea officinalis, valued for its thick, protective mucilage</note>, **egg white**, **psyllium seed** <note>original: *semen psilii*; another source of thick mucilage when soaked</note>, and **lime** <term>lime: Latin *calx*; calcium oxide, used here perhaps as a binding agent or to create a chemical crust</term>. Pulverize these and mix them with the egg white and the juice of a **radish**. 

Anoint your body or your hand with this mixture and let it dry; then, anoint it a second time. After this, you will be able to boldly endure fire without any injury. 

If you wish for the anointed part to actually **appear as if it is burning**, sprinkle it with well-pulverized **native sulfur** <note>original: *sulphure vivo*; "living" or naturally occurring sulfur, which ignites easily at low temperatures</note>, and it will seem to be consumed by flames when it is lit.

### To carry fire without harm
So that you can carry fire unhurt: let **lime** be dissolved in hot bean water, and add a little **red earth from Messina** <note>original: *terra rubea de missina*; a type of volcanic or ferruginous clay used in alchemy and medicine</note>. Afterward, add a small amount of **marshmallow** <term>marshmallow: Althaea officinalis; the roots and leaves produce a thick mucilage that acts as a heat barrier</term>. Once these are joined or mixed together, smear your palm with them and allow it to dry; in this way, you will be able to carry any fire whatsoever without being harmed.

### How to make burning water
You shall make **burning water** <note>original: *aquam ardentem*; this is a medieval recipe for aqua vitae or concentrated alcohol, though the addition of sulfur and salt suggests a highly flammable chemical mixture</note> in this way: take dark wine, thick and old, and in a fourth part of it you shall mix **quicklime**, finely powdered **virgin sulfur**, **tartar** from good wine <note>original: *tartari*; the potassium bitartrate crystals found in wine barrels</note>, and coarse white common salt. Afterward, place it in a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</term> that has been well-sealed with lute <note>original: *lutata*; a paste used to seal alchemical joints</note> and, having placed an **alembic** <term>alembic: the "head" or cap of a still used to collect and condense vapors</term> on top, you shall distill the burning water, which you ought to keep in a glass vessel.

### How to make Greek fire
You shall make **Greek fire** <note>original: *ignem græcum*; a legendary incendiary weapon that could burn on or under water, used famously by the Byzantine Empire</note> in this way: take virgin sulfur, tartar, **sarcocolla** <term>sarcocolla: a resinous gum from a Persian tree, historically used to "glue" flesh and in chemical recipes</term>, pitch, cooked salt, **petroleum**, and common oil. Boil these well; whatever is placed in it will catch fire, whether wood or iron, and it cannot be extinguished except with **urine**, **vinegar**, or **sand**.

<meta>This page continues the text of Albertus Magnus’s "On the Wonders of the World." It transitions from the physical recipes of the previous page into a philosophical explanation of why "wonders" occur, followed by the start of a recipe for a glowing stone.</meta>

<page-num>238</page-num>
<header>BOOK OF ALBERTUS MAGNUS</header>

...the **patient** <term>patient: from the Latin *patiens*, meaning the material that "undergoes" or receives an action, as opposed to the "agent" which performs it</term>, because if you consider both, you will not wonder. When you see such an aptitude in the sufficiency of one for the other, it does not cause wonder. For instance, when you see that cold water ignites fire and does not extinguish it: if you only looked at the **acting cause** <term>agent: the "efficient cause" or the force that triggers a change</term>, you would always be amazed, because it would seem to be an unsuitable force for such a task. But when you look at the **material** of that effect—such as **lime** <note>original: *calx*; specifically quicklime (calcium oxide), which reacts violently with water to produce intense heat</note> and **sulfur**, which is extremely flammable—you see that even the smallest trigger inflames it, and you see that it is not wonderful at all.

Similarly, when a thing is burned by fire, it seems wonderful only when one of the causes is inspected alone. But when the nature of the **patient** <gloss>the material being acted upon</gloss> or the weakness of the **agent** <gloss>the force acting upon it</gloss> is known, nothing is a wonder. Therefore, the greatest root of natural experiments consists in this: that they choose a material most ready for a certain effect, and pair it with a weak agent or a very strong one, or a material that is very poorly disposed to resist. They then make men look only at the cause which does not seem capable of producing that effect, and they say nothing of the material itself. Take note of this, for it is by this method that a multitude of "miraculous" experiments are performed. 

And of this I will tell you some examples so that you may be confirmed in the aforementioned power, and also so that you may know how to devise the ingenious mechanisms of experiments. If you wish to make a **carbuncle** <note>original: *carbunculum*; historically a red gemstone like a garnet or ruby, but in medieval alchemy, it often referred to a legendary "self-shining" stone</note> or a thing that shines in the night:

...take as many glowing **glow-worms** <note>original: *noctilucas*; literally "night-shiners," referring to fireflies or glow-worms</note> as possible and, having crushed them, place them in a glass vial. Once closed, bury them in warm **horse manure** <note>Manure was a staple in the alchemist's laboratory, used as a reliable way to provide a low, steady heat for "digestion" or fermentation.</note> and leave them to stay there for fifteen days. Afterward, you shall distill a water from them through an **alembic** <term>alembic: an early distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used to purify substances by heating them into vapor and condensing them back into liquid</term>, which you should store in a vessel of crystal or glass. Indeed, it provides such great clarity that in a dark place, anyone is able to read and write. Some make this water from glow-worms, the gall of a turtle, the gall of a weasel, the gall of a ferret, and a **water dog** <note>original: *canis aquatici*; likely referring to an otter or a seal</note>, burying them in manure and distilling water from them.

Also, mix it with wine or whatever you wish, and it is ignited if you bring a candle near it.

**Flying fire:** <note>This is a recipe for gunpowder, used here for early pyrotechnics or rockets.</note> Take one pound of **sulfur**, two pounds of **willow charcoal**, and six pounds of **saltpeter**. Let these three be ground very finely upon a marble stone; afterward, let a portion of the mixture be placed as desired into a paper **casing** <gloss>original: *tunica*; literally a "tunic" or "coat," here meaning the outer shell of the firework</gloss> for flying or for making thunder.

The casing for flying <note>i.e., a rocket</note> should be long and slender, and very well-filled with that powder; however, for making thunder <note>i.e., a firecracker or explosive</note>, it should be short, thick, and half-full.

### *To the Lord Frederick, Emperor*
### *of the Romans.*

**E**mperor, among the other things with which it is necessary for you to be concerned, is the knowledge of good and evil, and to investigate it in every way by yourself in the books of authors and in all sciences, and principally of those sciences which are called **arts** <term>arts: referring to the "Liberal Arts," the core curriculum of medieval education, consisting of the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy)</term>. And this you shall do thoroughly, when your soul is at rest and your body has a single space, having set aside the business of the people seeking something from your majesty and your responses to them. For you ought to know that there are two times for a living man: namely, a time of peace and a time of war; and likewise there are two foods: the bodily and the spiritual. The bodily food is prepared for the nourishment of the body. The spiritual food, however, is for the nourishment of the soul. It must be known that just as bodily food... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence here; the catchword "ralis" at the bottom of the original page indicates the word being completed on the next page is "corporalis," or "bodily."</note>

**...bodily** food preserves the body in a good state, if it is prepared with reason and taken in measure by the living being to whom it is suited, and at a suitable time: because not all things are suitable at all times. So spiritual food keeps the soul in a good state if it is prepared with reason and taken in due measure, at the appropriate time for each stage of life and virtue in a man. For it is written that just as cold things are tempered by hot and hot things by cold, so **opposites are cured by opposites** <term>opposites are cured by opposites: a translation of the medical maxim "contraria contrariis curantur," a fundamental principle of Galenic medicine suggesting that an illness caused by heat should be treated with cold</term>, and they receive healing in an orderly fashion. Wherefore, by my advice, you will naturally and courteously gather about you learned teachers, masters, and talented men; and you will often converse with many, speaking words wisely and familiarly in their presence. You will reflect on diverse matters for various reasons, and you will put questions to them when they are with you, and you will keep their sayings in your heart so that in the future they may benefit both you and others. ## The Utility of Physiognomy.

Noble Emperor, gracious man, as if possessing all graces and gifts, out of great love I make known to you the most sacred science of nature. This science can be called a consolation, and it is not often spoken of to ignorant peoples <note>original: "gentibus idiotis"; here referring to those lacking formal education or specialized knowledge rather than a modern medical definition</note>, nor indeed should it be told to them.

It is after the completion of fourteen years, and thereafter until the seventy-seventh year at most for a man, while in a female indeed after the completion of twelve years, and thereafter until forty or fifty years at most, that with this release of seed, hair begins to arise gradually on the pubic mound <note>original: *pectine*</note>, the junction of which is called the thigh. Similarly, hair grows in the nostrils of the nose, on the jaws of males <note>referring to the growth of the beard</note>, under the armpits, and around the sexual organs below, as well as on the arms, hands, and legs. This is just as the leaves begin to sprout in the time of spring on the trees, and flowers and branches on the herbs; for then the pores of the body are opened and produce something of their own kind.

Since women do not have within themselves as much <term>innate heat</term> <note>original: *calorem innatum*. If it is born in the **seventh month**, it survives well; it can survive because of the dominion of the **Moon**, since through her governance the order of duties from the planets is completed in such a creature. Indeed, once the order of operation of the **seven planets** is completed—which happens at the end of the seventh month—either the embryo is born and survives, or if it is not born, the aforementioned planets begin to reign over the creature again in the previously designated order. It should be known that one perceives how **Saturn** reigns in general in the **first month**, and so on. In the **eighth month**, he reigns again, etc. If it is born in the **eighth month**, the newborn does not survive, although it may be born alive and appropriately strong. This is due to the dominion of **Saturn** who then reigns: and who, by his coldness, chills the infant and shuts it in, as it is not willing to rise into the soul <note>original: *non volentem surgere in animam*; this likely refers to the animation or the "vital spark" being suppressed by Saturn's heavy, cold influence, preventing the child from truly "coming to life."</note>; hence it does not live beyond the eighth day.

## ON THE SECRETS OF NATURE.

...anyone born, whether early or late, has four inevitable **ailments** <note>original: *passiones*; in a medical context, these are "passions" or conditions the body suffers.</note>, namely **smallpox**, **scrofula** <note>original: *scurolas*; a swelling of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis in the Middle Ages.</note>, **fersae** <note>original: *fersas*; likely referring to measles or a similar eruptive skin rash.</note>, and **scabies**, whether wet or dry. And it should be known that the menstrual fluid is as necessary for conception as **alum** is for dye <note>original: *alumen tincturæ*; alum was a vital mineral used as a "mordant" to fix colors to fabric. Scot uses this as a metaphor: just as dye needs alum to stick to cloth, the male seed needs menstrual blood to "fix" into a human form.</note>; and unless there is some of it in the chamber where the conception occurs, the generation is not viable. 

Hence, if a creature is born and lives a long time, it is naturally purged of that impurity <note>The "impurity" refers to the leftover menstrual blood the fetus was exposed to in the womb, which medieval doctors believed was later expelled through the skin as the four diseases mentioned above.</note>. It should be known that if there was a flow when the conception took place, and too much menstrual fluid is created in the chamber, the child is conceived more or less corrupted; and then the man ought to abstain from intercourse, and the woman ought to resist him with wisdom. 

The course of this menstruation occurs when the **moon** is half or round <note>original: *rotunda*; meaning the full moon.</note>, and this flow sometimes lasts for one day, sometimes three or five, or more, depending on the lunar cycle and the condition of the amount of human vices. And it should be known that **Jews** naturally suffer a flow of blood through the penis <note>original: *virgam*; literally "rod," a common medieval euphemism for the penis.</note> according to the moon, in certain drops like women <note>This refers to the "male menstruation" myth, a common piece of medieval anti-Semitic pseudoscience used to "other" Jewish men by claiming they shared the perceived "infirmity" of women.</note>.

It should be known that as long as the infant is in the mother's womb, it lives on the **menstrual fluid**; that is, it feeds itself from it. It does not receive such nourishment through its mouth, but through the **umbilicus** <note>the navel or umbilical cord</note>. This is the reason why the menstrual blood flows at the usual time every month [in non-pregnant women]: because [during pregnancy] it is made into food for the embryo, and it has its course into the womb of the mother. 

This is sufficiently evident in a nursing woman and in a newborn child. A nursing woman does not suffer a menstrual flow except for some specific cause, because the **menstrual fluid is converted into milk**. <note>A standard belief in medieval medicine, following Aristotle and Galen, was that breast milk was simply "whitened" or "cooked" menstrual blood that traveled from the uterus to the breasts.</note> Furthermore, when the infant’s cord is cut from the navel, sometimes there is found in it the food which the mother ate that day. 

Once the infant is born, it is naturally nourished by milk until it is stronger. And while a woman remains a **virgin**, she may be recognized by the touch of the **tip of the nose** <note>original: *pilulæ nasi*; literally the "little ball" or cartilage at the end of the nose.</note>, because the cartilage is solid; but when she has been "corrupted by seed" <note>a medieval euphemism for the loss of virginity through sexual intercourse</note>, it is felt [to be soft or divided] in those parts.

**REGARDING** the exit of the infant, we say this: that each one comes out through the opening of the womb <note>original: *os vulvæ*; literally 'the mouth of the vulva'</note>; however, they come first with the head if they are quite healthy. It should be known that a male is born face up <note>original: *supinus*; lying on the back</note>, and if at any time he is held in bathwater and dies, he dies with his face downward; whereas a female is born not face up, but with her face downward, and if at any time she dies, it is face upward. <note>This passage reflects a medieval belief that the natural orientation of the sexes is inverted both in birth and in the way their bodies float or settle in water after death.</note> For [an infant] is born headfirst in any case, because this is for it a certain entrance into temporal life, so that it may see the world and recognize it as full of miseries and its own deficiency, and realize that of itself it can do nothing; and when it has died naturally, it is carried feet-first to the grave <note>original: *fossa*; a pit or ditch used for burial</note> as a sign of its end. And just as it entered the world through the head, so it is drawn out through the feet, seeing its end. But if it should be born otherwise, such as if a foot or hand comes out first, etc., it hardly survives. And it will die suddenly rather than escape, and its mother suffers pains and the dangers of death. But if the infant is turned <note>original: *versetur*; referring to a breech or transverse position</note> in the womb, it rarely happens that the woman escapes from that birth without dying. # ON THE THINGS WHICH HARM AND BENEFIT the fetus and the pregnant woman.

## CHAPTER XII.

**M**any things exist which harm the fetus <term>embryo</term> <note>While "embryo" is the original Latin term used here, it refers generally to the unborn child at any stage of development.</note> and not the mother, and vice versa, and some things harm both. Therefore, wishing to reveal this instruction, we say that the poppy plant <note>original: *papaver*</note> and its seed harm both. The reason is that they induce sleep in both, and the herb touches the skin of the fetus with a mark <note>original: *macula*; likely referring to a birthmark.</note> that never goes away. It should be known that the poppy and the little white rose produce white and red spots; therefore, a pregnant woman should not use them in food, lest the infant be lethargic or marked with spots. 

The meat of the hare and the lion harm the fetus greatly: because the hare always sleeps with its eyes open <note>This reflects the medieval belief in "maternal impressions," where the characteristics of the food eaten or sights seen by the mother were thought to be physically imprinted upon the child.</note>. Similarly, vinegar is harmful, as is *fulsus*—that is, the tendons of the feet of oxen—and milk and cucumber, because they induce excessive coldness <note>In the system of the four humors, pregnancy was seen as a delicate balance of heat; "cold" foods were thought to quench the natural heat required for the child's development.</note>, which brings danger to both. Cumin and saffron <note>original: *cafranum*</note> harm the fetus and dye its skin a pale color. Onions, garlic, lettuce, and dill harm the fetus, because it may lose its sight because of them.

For the chick is born twice—namely, first as an egg and afterwards as a chick, etc. Likewise, some animals are generated through sexual intercourse <term>coitu</term>, such as man and ox; others without intercourse, such as the eel, the crab, the scorpion, etc. <note>Medieval naturalists often believed in "spontaneous generation," where certain creatures were thought to arise from mud or decaying matter rather than mating.</note> The fly and the frog indeed mate, but they produce nothing. <note>This is an incorrect biological observation common in medieval texts; frogs were often thought to emerge from rain or mud.</note> Likewise, of all those being born, some are born alive and seeing, like man and ox; some blind, like the dog; some dead, like the bear <note>original: *ursus*. It was a popular medieval belief that bears gave birth to unformed, "dead" lumps of flesh that the mother then "licked into shape" to bring to life.</note>; some as a mere piece of flesh, like the lion; some powerful <note>original: *potens*. Likely referring to the physical maturity or mobility of the newborn.</note>, like the eagle and the greater part of animals; and some powerless, like man. 

It must be known that the blood of dogs and of infants of two months and younger, without a doubt, cures leprosy through a bath made of hot water. <note>This reflects the harsh and often shocking nature of medieval "sympathetic magic" and medicine, where the purity of an infant or the vitality of an animal was thought to transfer to the sick through ritual baths.</note> 

Regarding the love of the nourisher for the nourished and the nourished for the nurse, we say this: that an infant who is nourished in its own home, and principally by its mother, is loved more by its parents, and it loves them more than one who is nourished outside the home or by a foreign nurse. Because milk, labor, and habit <term>usus</term> <note>original: *usus*. Here referring to the psychological bonding caused by constant familiarity and shared routine.</note> cause this; hence one who is well-nourished in the home and by the mother loves the mother more at all times. But one who is nourished outside the home for a long time, when brought back into the home, is like a stranger...

**Why do parents love their son more than the son loves his parents?**
I respond: because the son is the flesh and blood of the parents, but not the reverse; hence, they have a pledge <term>pignus</term> <note>The term *pignus* suggests the child is a "token" or a biological investment of the parents' own substance.</note> in him, and he does not have the same in them. 

**Why does the mother love her son more ardently than the father, and feel more grief for his suffering, forgiving him for offenses committed?**
I respond: because she has more of her flesh and blood in him, and she has maintained companionship and friendship with him more and for a longer time by carrying him in her womb and outside of it, as well as by nourishing him with milk, etc. 

**Why does the father love the son more than the mother?** <note>Scotus provides an alternative perspective here, focusing on physical resemblance rather than the duration of care.</note>
I respond: because the seed of the man was more [prevalent] in him, and he is more similar to the same father than to the mother. 

**Why do a father and mother not maintain hostility <term>guerram</term> <note>original: *guerram*, literally "war." In this context, it refers to a persistent grudge or family feud.</note> against a son as firmly and as long as a son does against them?**
I respond: because he is their flesh and blood, and not the reverse. Since they have long been accustomed to that habit, treatment, and the nourishment provided by their own labor, and have granted him so much, this is why it happens. 

**Why do parents love the first-born more than the others?**
I respond: because the child is a new experience; and if it were not a natural law that the small should be so loved, many would perish. <note>Scotus argues that parental affection is a survival mechanism designed by nature to ensure helpless infants are cared for.</note>

## *HOW IT MAY BE KNOWN how many children each woman ought to have, having seen the first birth.*

### CHAPTER XVIII.

**S**o that anyone may know how many children any woman is destined to have after observing the first birth, we say that if the infant has emerged from its mother's womb and has dropped down and been lifted from the spot by the <term>midwife</term> <note>original: *obstetricem*; in the Middle Ages, midwives were the primary medical authorities on childbirth and the care of newborns.</note>, the knots of that <term>umbilical cord</term> <note>original: *umbilici*.</note> which is attached to the womb must be examined; and however many knots there are, that is how many children she is still able to have and carry.

## *known in a pregnant woman whether the embryo is healthy or infirm, likely to live long enough, or to die quickly, both within the womb and outside.*

To this discourse, we add this teaching: that thinness of the breasts in a woman signifies a scarcity of milk. Also, milk from the right breast is better than that from the left.

## ON ANIMALS IN GE-
## neral and in species.

### CHAPTER 20.

The differences among animals, both in their general kind and in their specific species, are manifold—namely in their nature, their properties, the nourishment of their food, and the physical differences of their limbs, and the fact that they relate to many and diverse things. Therefore, it should be known that among animals—whether two-footed, four-footed, and so forth—some are born only once, such as man and the ox. Others, however, are born twice: such as the rooster and the pigeon; that is to say, first as an egg, and afterwards as a chick. Some are born three times, such as the butterfly <term>papilio</term> <note>original: *papilio*; used here to describe the life cycle of winged insects.</note>, because first it reproduces, and the caterpillar <term>eruca</term> <note>original: *eruca*; a larva or caterpillar.</note> makes an "egg" in a small pod <note>original: *folliculum*; referring to a cocoon or chrysalis. The author views the cocoon as a second "egg" stage.</note>, and from that a worm is born, which, having turned into a butterfly, breaks the pod and flies. Likewise, some are born small and stay small, while others are made large, such as the dog, the cat, the lamb, the pig, man, and the ox; some are made the largest of all, like the elephant. Also, some are domestic, and some are intermediate between the two. It should be known that there are some that are quickly domesticated, and some slowly and with difficulty. Those that are born domestic are humans, dogs, and sheep. Those which are truly wild <term>silvatica</term> <note>literally "of the woods."</note> are fleas <note>original: *pulices*; medieval natural history often grouped small insects with "wild" animals as they were not under human control.</note>, hares, and crabs. Those, however, which are born partly domestic and partly wild <meta>catchword: -strial (completing 'silvestria' / 'terrestrial')</meta>

## CHAPTERS 22 AND 23.

->308<-

**R**eturning to the doctrine of **physiognomy** <term>physiognomia</term> <note>Physiognomy was a popular medieval science based on the idea that a person's outward appearance, especially the face, revealed their inner character and the state of their soul.</note> in humans and beasts, we say that souls follow the body, and these souls are not, in and of themselves, susceptible to the motions of the body in which they dwell for a certain span of temporal life. At the end of this life, they are separated and the body remains. This connection is manifest in the excessive motions caused by the drunkenness of wine, or by love, or by the sadness of labor and illness. ...proper signs <note>In medieval science, "proper signs" (signa propria) are specific indicators belonging to an individual or species that reveal hidden truths, as opposed to "common signs" which are obvious to everyone.</note> only, which—although all men could possess them—nevertheless do not all have them within themselves. For who is in doubt regarding common signs and those things which no one is ignorant of? Therefore, it is not fitting for a wise man to state a common sign in front of anyone; for instance, if seeing a man who is clearly strong through experience, he were to say "that man is as strong as a lion." It is already well known that he is as strong as a lion, and so forth.

For we must wisely determine each and every thing that properly provides the science of <term>physiognomizing; the practice of determining a person's character or fate from their physical features</term>, so that through this science, whoever masters it—as we shall plainly describe in the following sections—may be of worth among the people and attain all reverence and honor of reputation, along with profit. For each of those things that provide a <term>physiognomy; a systematic reading of the body's appearance</term> in men are those things found in them from the habits of the body: namely, from the form or figure by comparison to any limb, and also from color, from the lightness or heaviness of gait, from posture, and from voice, etc.

...of the members <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of "simple" and "composite" body parts.</note> under their own headings as it seems fit to us, and as it has seemed to certain others—such as Hippocrates, Galen, and Al-Mansur <note>original: "Alminsori"; referring to the Persian physician Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, who dedicated a famous medical text to the governor Al-Mansur. But before we come to the full intent of our discourse, we say by way of a primary rule <note>original: "ex prærogativa," implying a foundational warning or priority for the student of physiognomy</note> that one must at all times be very wary of meeting or keeping company with an "unfortunate" man—one who is a work of the higher nature <note>original: "opus naturæ superioris," referring to astrological or cosmic influences that shape a person's destiny and physical form at birth</note>—such as a man who is diminished in some limb, like an eye, a hand, and so forth. 

The reason is because any such person is made unhappy, and out of his own misfortune, he hinders the fortunate. And in this regard, he presents a harm in many ways that is hidden from the ignorant man, since that man cannot weigh this matter properly except by way of this doctrine <note>The science of physiognomy</note> or through the experience of his own misfortune. For every man can better guard himself against his public enemy after an offense has been committed than he can against an unfortunate man. The reason is that harm in fortune is hidden, while the harm of an enemy is public. 

And it should be known that there is no creature of such a good <term>complexion; the balance of bodily humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—that determines a person's health and temperament</term> that, if a limb is diminished, his state does not change, either for the worse (which is common) or much for the better (which rarely happens) if he lives a long time. Hence it is said: "Beware of those who are marked." And elsewhere: "In a man marked in any limb, do not place your trust." <note>This reflects a common medieval prejudice that physical disabilities or "marks" were outward signs of internal moral failings or bad luck ordained by the heavens.</note>

## SIGNS OF THE TEMPERAMENT
->By reason of the color in the face.<-

### CHAPTER 24.

**A** white color in the face, or a dark color mixed with a sort of whiteness and bluish-gray—or even a chalky and leaden color—naturally signifies a cold temperament <note>term: "complexionem" (complexion/temperament). In medieval medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which dictated a person’s health and personality.</note>. A red or reddish color in the face, composed with whiteness and many freckles, signifies a hot temperament. A white color in the face, accompanied by gentle manners and an intermixed redness, signifies a balanced temperament. A bluish or sallow color in the skin, and also in the fingernails, signifies a bad and cold temperament.

->By reason of the color in the skin.<-

**A** body that is white in the skin and dry in the flesh, having some or much red color in appropriate places, signifies the dominance of red bile <note>original: "choleræ rubeæ." Also known as yellow bile, this humor was thought to be hot and dry, making a person "choleric"—ambitious, brave, or easily angered.</note>. A body that is thick in the flesh and white in the skin, and appropriately colored, signifies the dominance <note>The text likely continues to discuss the dominance of "blood," which characterizes the sanguine temperament.</note>

# SIGNS OF A BODY OF A MOIST <term>complexion</term>.
<note>In medieval science, "complexion" refers to the unique balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's physical and mental nature.</note>
## CHAPTER XXVIII.

**B**odies that are naturally moist are soft and smooth in their flesh; their <term>joints</term> <note>original: "juncturæ". In physiognomy, hidden joints were a sign of abundant flesh and fluid, while visible joints suggested dryness.</note> are hidden and possess little strength. For this reason, they can endure little labor; they are timid and fearful of almost everything, and they sleep poorly. They are often moved toward <term>lust</term> <note>original: "luxuriam". Medieval physicians believed that excess bodily fluids (moisture) stimulated sexual desire.</note>. They are bare of body hair. Their eyes are always watering. Their body hair and the hair on their heads are straight and fine, and they have a good <term>natural talent</term> <note>original: "ingenii" (intellect or disposition). A "moist" brain was often thought to be more receptive to new impressions and learning.</note> for learning.

# SIGNS OF A BODY OF A DRY <term>complexion</term>.
## CHAPTER XXIX.

**B**odies that are naturally dry are felt to be rough to the touch; they are lean in flesh, but strong and durable in labor; they eat willingly and appropriately; the joints of their limbs are prominent and visible. Their head hair and body hair are thick, rough, and curly.

# SIGNS OF A <term>BALANCED</term>
# *and healthy body.*

## *CHAPTER XXX.*

**B**odies that are balanced and healthy eat and drink well according to their needs; they digest and manage their affairs <note>The Latin "disponunt res" implies both physical regulation of the body and the orderly management of one's life.</note> appropriately and have good judgment. This implies a lack of refinement or a "thick" understanding.</note>. His hair is light and straight, grows slowly, and is white or almost leaden in color. His eyes are rarely moved, and he sees but briefly; he is a great waker by night, of stable purpose, tenacious in labor, and generous within reason. To the touch, he feels cold and soft; he is of subtle wit and somewhat shrewd for learning.

The man is hot in his flesh, has a good appetite, is bold in his deeds, harsh in his speech, and stingy in giving. He is also stubborn, proud, prone to anger, and <term>lustful</term> <note>original: "luxuriosus." Medieval scholars believed that "heat" in the heart fueled sexual desire and physical passion.</note>.

If the heart is of a **cold constitution**, the pulse is slow, the chest is bare of hair, and the flesh is cold to the touch. He has a poor appetite and weak strength; his breathing is constricted, and his voice is thin and weak. He is, as it were, lazy in his actions and not very pleasant in his speech. He is easily frightened, does not eat well, and is rarely lustful, unless it occurs <term>by accident</term> <note>original: "per accidens." This is a philosophical/medical term meaning "by chance" or due to external circumstances—such as eating certain foods or drugs—rather than his natural temperament.</note>.

If the heart is of a **moist constitution**, the man abounds with much hair because it grows long and straight very quickly. In color, the hair is white or pale. He has plenty of hair elsewhere, except on the chest; his flesh is soft to the touch, and his skin color is white or dusky. He is also somewhat fat, very timid, fearful, dull, and weak when it comes to labor.

# ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE PARTS
## *of the body in every animal.*

**T**he heart is naturally hotter than all other members of the body, and by its heat the whole body is given life; it maintains heat in the rest of its parts, receiving it from a higher influence <note>The "higher influence" refers to the medieval belief that the heart received vital spirit or celestial heat to distribute to the body.</note> through which the body remains a cohesive whole. Because the other parts of the body are warmed by the heat of the heart, we can say that the heart is the fountain and origin of innate heat. Fat is naturally colder and drier, consisting of a certain thickened moisture. Bone is naturally hot and dry. Marrow is naturally hot and moist. # SIGNS OF AN EXCESS
## *of bad humors.*
### CHAPTER 39.

An <term>excess</term> <note>original: "repletio." # SIGNS OF EXCESSIVE
## BLOOD.
### CHAPTER 40.

**W**hen blood abounds too much, itching occurs almost everywhere on the flesh, and primarily in the arms. An abundance of redness appears in the face, and a sweetness is constantly tasted in the mouth, more than is usual. Blisters form in the mouth and on the lips, and certain burnings are felt in the chest which we call <term>carbuncles</term> <note>original: "carbunculos." While today this refers to a cluster of boils, in medieval medicine it could also refer to internal "burning" inflammations or sores caused by "overheated" blood.</note>, because of which the person loses their appetite and their sleep. The urine is red and somewhat thick, the body grows fat, and foods taste good when eaten; for this reason, the person has a good appetite, and digests and <term>disposes</term> <note>original: "disponit." This refers to the body's ability to distribute nutrients and manage waste effectively.</note> well.

## Cholera.

# SIGNS OF EXCESSIVE 
# MELANCHOLY.

## CHAPTER XLIII.

**W**hen <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: "melancholia." In medieval medicine, this is the humor associated with Black Bile, characterized as cold and dry.</note> reigns too much, there occurs a <term>burning of the stomach</term> <note>original: "ardor stomachi," likely referring to heartburn or acid reflux.</note>, a great <term>voracious hunger</term> <note>original: "appetitus canini." Literally "dog-like appetite," describing an intense, pathological craving for food.</note>, a dark color in the face, and the blood is black and thick. The urine is black, or somewhat reddish, tending slightly toward greenness or paleness. The body feels cold to the touch, the person is sluggish in labor, and the feet are cold. The heart is very suspicious, and the person is sad in thought, easily angered, <term>clinging</term> <note>original: "tenax." This can mean stubborn or, more commonly in descriptions of the melancholic temperament, miserly and unwilling to let go of money or possessions.</note>, loving to remain in solitude, and taking little food and drink.

# A BRIEF DOCTRINAL
# NOTE.

## CHAPTER XLIIII.

**N**ature does nothing in vain, and in each thing she always does what is best; therefore, no quality is idle in the body. # ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF AUGURIES.
## CHAPTER LVI.

**A**uguries <note>original: "auguria." While the term originates with ancient Roman religious officials who observed birds, in this medieval context it refers more broadly to any natural sign or omen believed to predict the future.</note> are found mentioned in the <term>canons of the church</term> <note>original: "canonibus ecclesias." This refers to ecclesiastical laws. The Church generally condemned the practice of augury as superstition or paganism, yet many medieval scholars continued to study it as a branch of "natural science."</note>; nevertheless, we say that certain signs are received through the encountering of a person or another animal, or by the hearing of a voice. An **augur** (a term used for both men and women) is one who, through such knowledge, indicates future things, and thus through the specific signs of this science, knows and understands how to judge each thing according to its kind.

Hence, it should be known that some auguries signify a good outcome, some a bad outcome, and some a middle ground between the two. For there are certain notable things in which auguries are properly observed, such as:
*   <term>sneezing</term> <note>original: "sternutatio." Historically, sneezing was one of the most common omens, often requiring a blessing (like "God bless you") to ward off potential evil.</note>
*   yawning
*   encountering the flight of birds
*   the singing of birds
*   a spoken word <note>original: "vox edita locutionis." This refers to "cledonism," the practice of taking a chance remark overheard from a stranger as a prophetic sign regarding one's current business.</note> concerning a proposed business matter
*   or a preceding dream.

In this way, a human being creates an augury for another human, just as other animals do—such as the eagle, the <term>crow</term> <note>original: "cornicula."</note>, the <term>night-owl</term> <note>original: "nicticorax." Furthermore, some auguries are observed behind, some on the right, and some on the left, since they are diverse in their arrangement—whichever... <note>The text ends mid-sentence, continuing to the next page.</note>

**S**ternuto, sternutas <note>original: "Sternuto, as"</note> is a verb, and it means "to sneeze." ...[business] <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of business dealings.</note> if he makes two <term>sneezes</term> <note>original: "sternutationes"</note>, or four, or if they were made elsewhere by another person, and he immediately rises if he was sitting, and if he immediately moves his feet and begins to go to complete his business or to undertake it, he will prosper in it. # ON THE EYEBROWS.
<note>original: "De Ciliis." While "cilia" can mean eyelashes in modern biology, in medieval physiognomy it typically refers to the eyebrows or the general orbital region.</note>
## CHAPTER 61.

Eyebrows that are highly arched and frequently raised upward signify a person who is proud, <term>high-spirited</term> <note>original: "animosum," often implying a person of strong passions or courage</note>, vain, boastful, audacious, threatening, a desirer of beautiful things, and adaptable to both extremes <note>original: "convenientem ad utraque," meaning they are capable of both good and evil deeds or can fit into any situation</note>. One whose eyebrows are turned downwards when they speak to or look at another—as if hiding beneath them—signifies a person who is very malicious or a deceitful liar, a traitor, <term>stingy</term> <note>original: "tenacem," literally "holding fast," often used for greed or miserliness</note>, lazy, secretive, and a person of few words. One whose eyebrows have sparse hairs signifies a person who is simple, vain, weak, gullible, and a fairly agreeable companion. One whose eyebrows are naturally folded downwards, appearing almost without a curve, signifies a person who is unlearned, lazy, suspicious, stingy, envious, and in many matters, easily a deceiver. One whose eyebrows are very short and white or <term>leaden</term> <note>original: "plumbea," a dull, grayish color</note> in color signifies a person who is adaptable to almost anything, timid, easily and quickly trusting of others—and likewise the reverse <note>original: "et e converso," suggesting the opposite traits may also manifest or that they are equally easy to deceive</note>.

# ON THE SPACE BETWEEN THE EYEBROWS.
## CHAPTER 62.

**T**he space between the eyebrows <term>intercilia</term> <note>original: "Intercilia," the glabellar region above the bridge of the nose where the eyebrows meet</note> signifies a person who is <term>stingy</term> <note>original: "tenacem," literally "holding fast," often used by Scot to denote a miserly or greedy nature</note>, envious, secretive, shrewd, and greatly desiring of beautiful things; they are prone to empty fortune, and are more cruel than pleasant. One whose space between the eyebrows is very long <note>original: "longa valde," suggesting a wide gap between the brows</note> signifies a person of somewhat <term>slow understanding</term> <note>original: "durae capacitatis," literally "hard capacity," referring to someone who is difficult to teach or slow to grasp new concepts</note>, yet of a subtle intellect, great boldness, much happiness, and clear and perfect friendship.

# ON THE EYES.
## CHAPTER 63.

**L**arge eyes—that is, thick or bulging ones—signify a person who is frequently lazy, sometimes bold, envious, partially bashful and partially unable to keep a secret, adaptable, stingy, vain, a casual liar, prone to great anger, of bad memory, of coarse wit and little intellect, and possessing less wisdom because he <term>refuses to learn</term> <note>original: "se repudet scire," implying a willful rejection of knowledge or a lack of intellectual curiosity</note>. One whose eyes are deep-set within the head and far-seeing signifies a person who is suspicious, malicious, prone to great anger, perverse in manners, of very good memory, bold, and cruel.

# CONCERNING THE NOSE.

## CHAPTER LXIV.

**A** **long and somewhat thin** nose signifies a man who is bold, curious in his actions, easily angered, vain, quickly swayed, weak in either direction <note>original: "ad utrunque debilem," perhaps meaning he lacks resolve in both good and bad ventures</note>, and easily believing what he is told. 

One whose nose is **long and extended with the tip pointing downward** signifies a man who is shrewd, secretive, helpful, reasonably faithful, honest, and a <term>supplanter</term> <note>original: "subplantaneum," implying someone who is cunning or capable of tripping up others in his dealings</note> in his affairs. 

One who is **snub-nosed** <note>original: "simus," referring to a flat or upturned nose</note> signifies an impetuous man, vain, a liar, lustful, weak, unstable, quickly believing others, and easily swayed in either direction. 

One whose nose is **wide in the middle and slopes toward its tip** signifies a man who is prone to lying, vain, lustful, talkative, and of cruel fortune. 

One whose nose is **thick all over and quite long** signifies a man who is a lover of all beautiful things, simple regarding good things but reasonably wise in bad things, quite fortunate, fervent in the things he desires, secretive, and knowing significantly less than he considers himself to know. 

One whose nose is **very sharp at the tip and of medium size**—between long and short, or thick and thin <note>The text ends mid-word with "sub-," likely intending "subtilem" (thin/slender) to complete the contrast with "grossum" (thick).</note>—

# ON THE MOUTH.
## CHAPTER LXVI.

A **large and wide mouth**, both in its closing and opening, signifies a man who is bold, shameless, easily provoked to war, a liar, wordy, a <term>news-monger</term> <note>original: "novigerulum," referring to a gossip or someone who constantly carries tales and news</note>, a heavy eater of <term>unrefined nature</term> <note>original: "grossi ingenii," suggesting a person with a crude or unpolished intellect</note>, stingy, and very foolish. One whose **mouth is small** in its closing and opening signifies a man who is peaceful, timid, faithful, secretive, tenacious yet generous, modest, learned, and who eats little. One whose **mouth has foul breath** signifies a man with a diseased liver <note>In medieval medicine, bad breath was often attributed to vapors rising from a "vicious" or unbalanced liver</note>, who is often a liar, vain, lustful, deceptive, of slight capacity, of coarse intellect, a seducer, envious, greedy, and appropriately generous to others, a news-monger, quickly withdrawing, and more simple than wise. One whose **mouth has sweet-smelling breath** signifies a man who is moderate in giving and keeping, shrewd, secretive, fair, quick to believe, and easily adaptable to both sides.

## ON THE LIPS.
### CHAPTER LXVII.

**L**ips of the mouth that are very thick or excessively rolled outward signify a man who is more simple than wise, quick to believe, of <term>unrefined nourishment</term> <note>original: "grossi nutrimenti"; in medieval thought, the type of food one digested was believed to correspond to the refinement of their character and intellect</note>, and adaptable to either side <note>meaning easily influenced toward either good or evil</note>. One whose lips are suitably thin and not very turned outward signifies a man who is discreet, secretive in all things, shrewd, prone to anger, and of great <term>natural talent</term> <note>original: "multi ingenii," referring to a sharp or multifaceted intellect</note>. One whose lips are well-colored and more thin than thick signifies a man of good character, easily adaptable to either side in all things, but more quickly moved toward virtues than toward vices. One whose lips are not well-balanced in everything, such that one is larger than the other, signifies a man who is more simple than wise, of unrefined intellect, slow understanding, and of varying fortune.

...[the superflu]ity of which rises up to the parts of the jaws like smoke to the openings of a chimney. And when it no longer finds open passages through which it can easily ascend further, they emerge from there in the form of hairs, which are called the hairs of the **beard**.

Almost all women lack a beard on their jaws. And it should be known that all those <term>humors</term> <note>the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern health and character</note> from which the beard is generated in men, [become] in women the **menses**, which occur through a certain passage and by the movement of the moon's cycle, sometimes once a month, and sometimes twice. The exit of this is called a flow or a <term>superfluity</term> <note>original: "superfluū"; in medieval medicine, a waste product or leftover of the body's metabolic processes</note>. This happens when a woman is not pregnant once she is past 12 years of age; and this menstrual fluid is sometimes even transmuted into milk within the breasts <note>this reflects the medieval medical theory that breast milk was purified menstrual blood</note>. 

It is true that these humors are so subtle and hot by nature that hairs sometimes arise from them on the jaws of a woman, and specifically around the mouth where heat is more abundant, and such a woman is said to be **bearded**. It should be known that such a woman is very <term>lustful</term> <note>original: "luxuriosa"; in this context, implying a high sexual drive driven by internal "heat"</note> because of her hot <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionē"; the specific balance of humors in an individual's body which determines temperament</note>. She is therefore of a strong nature and a virile condition.

However, a woman who is well-cleansed of hairs, and especially around the mouth, is said according to <term>physiognomy</term> <note>the pseudo-scientific practice of judging character from physical features</note> to be of a good complexion: namely timid, fearful, modest, weak, mild, and obedient—and the bearded woman is the opposite. [A person] either already has a beard or does not; if they have one, it has been discussed, but if they have no beard at all, this must be explained as being for one who lacks it, either because they are not yet of an age to have one, or there is a specific cause why it can never emerge. # ON THE FACE.

One whose belly is small and stretched signifies a man who is industrious, reasonably steady, shrewd, of good understanding, and of a <term>tender capacity</term> <note>original: "teneræ capacitatis"; a term used in medieval physiognomy to describe a mind that is impressionable, quick to perceive, but perhaps lacking in robust "hardness" or stubbornness</note>. ...backwards because it lacks a tail. It should be known that Aristotle says in the *Book of Animals* <note>original: "libro animalium"; referring to Aristotle's *History of Animals*, a foundational text for medieval science</note>, "Every animal lacking a great amount of flesh on its legs has a tail of some substance, such as hair, etc." <note>Aristotle’s logic here is based on the "law of compensation": nature reallocates physical matter from one part of the body to another.</note> One whose legs are thick with bone and flesh, and are hairy, signifies a man who is strong, bold, wise, and confident, but also of a coarse wit, lazy, slow, and of <term>hard capacity</term> <note>original: "duræ capacitatis"; a medieval term for someone who is slow to learn or intellectually stubborn</note>. One whose legs are entirely bare of hair signifies a man who is chaste, weak, and easily frightened. One whose legs are very hairy signifies a man who is also hairy around the genitals and is lustful, often vain, simple, and unstable, abounding in <term>bad humors</term> <note>In medieval physiology, "humors" were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that governed health and personality.</note>.

...how hasty [men are] to enter this same science, since judgment should not be based on just one of these [features] alone. Instead, every <term>physiognomist: a scholar who interprets character and fate from physical appearance</term> ought to cautiously gather for himself the evidence of the entire body—specifically those signs which are not altered by accidental circumstances, such as changes in a person’s state of health. These include the evidence provided by the eyes, forehead, nose, ears, teeth, and so forth.

And when these various signs provide a basis for the judgment and the merit of Physiognomy, one must always lean toward a universal perspective and the judgment of the majority of all the <note>original: "membrorum," literally members or body parts</note> which we have categorized above. He who acts otherwise will easily fall into error. 

The reason for this is that every individual part of the body contains its own specific indicators, as is clear from the preceding chapters. Therefore, no man can be judged by a single indicator from a single part, because one sign may contradict another. In these cases, the stronger evidence must overcome and conquer the weaker. 

Because the body parts are many, and each possesses its own indicators, the individual chapters of this book do not seem to be in error, even though no single man perfectly matches any one description we have given. Indeed, an individual will often appear to vary greatly from the "whole" type; if this were not the case, there could be no just or accurate proof. The eyes have their own signs, and based on the eyes alone, a man might be judged to have a certain disposition. But the other parts of the body also speak. Therefore, since there are so many parts, there are likewise [many signs to consider]...
